TITLE: cacher watch timeout not handled when it is not ready
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

In one of our multi tenant cluster, we've observed that all kubelet requests (under `system-nodes` flow schema) eventually started timing out or aborted due to secret watch request occupying all `system` priority level concurrency share. It happened due to our KMS provider was quite latent (& sometimes failing) for brief amount of time. Due to high latency from KMS provider, all the cacher's reflector list & watch calls start failing (repeatedly retried) and cacher was marked as not ready.

Now all the watch request to the cacher was waiting for `ready` conditional variable and never timed out. This led all watch requests stuck in priority and fairness queue for ever & eventually occupying all the concurrency shares, affecting other requests belonging to same priority level.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f173d01c011c3574dea73a6fa3e20b0ab94531bb/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L457-L467

We need to handle watch timeout when cacher not ready to fix the issue.

### What did you expect to happen?

Watch requests to get time out eventually when cacher is not ready.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and p
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the cacher's readiness blocking mechanism was implemented using a sync.Cond variable that did not support context cancellation or timeouts. As a result, watch requests waiting for the cacher to become ready could be blocked indefinitely if the cacher was never marked ready, leading to infinite wait and resource exhaustion in concurrency queues.
FIX: cacher allow context cancellation if not ready

TITLE: client-go: the retry logic in rest.Request should be thread safe

So the goal is to fix it in 1.25 and then back port all the way to 1.22.

Please note that there are other members (not related to retry logic) of `Request` that are not thread safe depending on how different methods of a `Request` object is used from multiple go routines.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102217/files#r837633535

Also, the comments on some of these methods and sections for retry logic can be improved:
- For instance, we may want to rename `IsErrorRetryable` to `IsHttpErrRetryable` and `checkWait` to `isServerIndicatedRetry`. 
That would have helped bring this back into mental cache faster and possibly help some future refactorer.

Maintain thread safety of `*Request`

This design allowed concurrent goroutines to share and modify the same retry state, violating the previous thread safety guarantees of the `Request` methods.

diagnosis.root_cause: The root defect is that the lengthDelimitedFrameReader in the watch stream masks client timeout errors as io.ErrShortBuffer (code-2). This masking causes the watch stream error handling in StreamWatcher to misinterpret these timeouts as internal server errors instead of retriable watch timeouts (code-3). Consequently, the reflector treats these errors as InternalError that it does not retry but immediately relists (code-1). This causes expensive and unnecessary relist operations instead of resuming the watch, despite the original error being recoverable by retry. The improper error masking prevents the correct classification of errors for retry logic.

claims.text: The lengthDelimitedFrameReader masks client timeout errors by replacing the original timeout error with io.ErrShortBuffer when no bytes are read (n==0), obscuring the true nature of the error.

Because the StreamWatcher.Receive method checks for retryable errors using net.IsTimeout(err), the masking leads the method to classify these client timeouts as StatusInternalServerError events, causing the reflector to trigger a costly relist instead of resuming the watch.

The reflector code’s retry mechanism returns false for ShouldRetry in presence of InternalError with io.ErrShortBuffer error, causing it to perform a relist immediately on this recoverable error type instead of retrying the watch.

TITLE: Scheduling Pods with dynamic resources and using the Pod `.spec.nodeName` field fails
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The combination of using the Pod spec nodeName field with the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin (currently feature-gated) doesn't work. No surprise really as the nodeName field effective bypasses the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin running, and something rather clever would need to be invented to make things to work. But this is still a bit of a regression compared to the old device plugin model which doesn't have a similar limitation.  @pohly as the author of the dynamic resources feature can explain what could maybe be created to fix this.

Granted, forcing scheduling even with a device plugin resource may or may not succeed at the node level depending on the availability of said plugin resources at the node, but with dynamic resources the failure seems to be currently guaranteed.

The use-case for this is such that the Kubernetes scheduler is effectively being preceded by some other scheduler which runs earlier (say, some HPC framework) which is giving the Pods the node names and somehow knows that there will be enough resources, and then the workloads ought to land in the specified node and the container related work is then handled normally from t
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that when a Pod has its spec.nodeName field set (indicating it is pre-assigned to a specific node), the Dynamic Resources scheduler plugin is bypassed and does not run. Since this plugin is responsible for managing resource claims and reservations, bypassing it leads to the pod being rejected or failing to run because its resource claims are not properly allocated or reserved. This limitation arises because the scheduler plugin is skipped when the pod is pre-scheduled, preventing the dynamic resource allocation logic from executing.
FIX: kube-controller-manager: the dynamic resource controller steps in when a pod got created such that the scheduler ignores it (i.e. spec.nodeName is set) and then takes care of triggering delayed resource claim allocation and/or reserving a claim for the pod.

TITLE: Flag to Disable the 6-minute Force Detach Window
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Certain online upgrade workflows might need to restart kubernetes as a part of their upgrade procedure. This can lead to the following sequence:
* As a part of draining a kubernetes node, a pod might get deleted.
* The unmount of a pod could take more than 6 minutes.
* If the node is deemed unhealthy when the 6 minute timer fires for the pod being deleted (for example, because kubelet is still restarting), then the underlying PV will be force detached (via a `ControllerUnpublishVolume` RPC)

These workflows would likely benefit from disabling this feature in lieu of the Non-Graceful Node Shutdown feature that hit GA in kubernetes 1.28 (see [here](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2023/08/16/kubernetes-1-28-non-graceful-node-shutdown-ga/) for more details).

When these issues are encountered in our testbeds, we are left with Zombie iSCSI LUNs. If pods end up migrating to a node with such a Zombie LUN present, those pods might end up attaching themselves to the Zombie LUN leading to data corruption.

This data corruption has caused a number of our cluster-management applications to lose all access to their data, requiring them to be deployed from scratch (occasi
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurs because there is a built-in 6-minute timeout after which volumes are force detached if the node is unhealthy, regardless of whether the pod has successfully unmounted the volume. This force detachment can cause persistent volumes to become stuck in a 'Zombie' state, leading to data corruption when pods attach to these stale volumes. The root cause is the rigid 6-minute force detach window that triggers detach operations without accounting for longer unmount durations and node restart circumstances.
FIX: This change adds the following CLI option for `kube-controller-manager`:
* `disable-force-detach` (defaults to `false`): Prevent force detaching volumes based on maximum unmount time and node status. diagnosis.root_cause: Starting with Kubernetes 1.30, the kubectl exec command defaults to using the WebSocket protocol for remote command execution. The WebSocket connection implements heartbeat pings every 5 seconds and a read deadline of about 1 minute, but the specific disconnection after 5 minutes is caused by a session timeout related to WebSocket handling. Disabling the RemoteCommandWebsockets feature (e.g., setting KUBECTL_REMOTE_COMMAND_WEBSOCKETS=false) circumvents this by reverting to the prior SPDY method, which does not disconnect sessions prematurely. This indicates that the disconnect behavior is rooted in the WebSocket executor's heartbeat and connection timeout logic introduced in 1.30.

claims.text: Kubectl exec in versions 1.30.x uses WebSocket protocol for remote command execution by default, controlled by the RemoteCommandWebsockets feature gate.
WebSocketExecutor in kubectl implements heartbeat pings every 5 seconds and a read deadline of about 1 minute, setting a strict timeout pattern on websocket connections.

The issue of sessions disconnecting after 5 minutes occurs only in versions 1.30.x with WebSocket enabled, and setting KUBECTL_REMOTE_COMMAND_WEBSOCKETS=false disables the new WebSocket executor, preventing these premature disconnections.

TITLE: Transition running deleted pods to a terminal phase
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Running pods when deleted are not transitioned to a terminal phase, even when all containers are terminated. Note that, containers are not restarted for deleted pods: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go#L73-L77.

This is problematic for jobs, which as a workaround categorizes all deleted pods (with `deletionTimestamp != nil`) as failed,
but it is still problematic:
- the replacement pod is created too early, leaving two running pods (for the same index) at the same time, which is a problem for some job frameworks. See related Issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115844.
- a pod categorized a failed by the job controller (due to the presence of deletionTimestamp) may end up succeeded if the pod's container completes successfully within the graceful termination period. 
- it blocks a related issue in Jobs: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113855.

The solution might be scoped to pods with finalizers to save a PATCH request to make the transitioning. 

Fixing this issue is planned as part of the Jobs KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3329

### What 
ROOT CAUSE: The kubelet did not transition deleted pods that are still in the Running or Pending phase to a terminal phase (Succeeded or Failed) even when their containers had terminated and would not be restarted due to their RestartPolicy. This caused deleted pods to remain stuck in Running or Pending state indefinitely.
FIX: Give terminal phase correctly to all pods that will not be restarted. 

In particular, assign Failed phase to pods which are deleted while pending. Also, assign a terminal 
phase (Succeeded or Failed, depending on the exit statuses of the pod containers) to pods which
are deleted while running.

This fixes the issue for jobs using pod failure policy (with JobPodFailurePolicy and PodDisruptionConditions 
feature gates enabled) that their pods could get stuck in the pending phase when deleted.

ACTION REQUIRED: Users who maintain controllers which relied on the fact that pods with RestartPolicy=Always
never enter the Succeeded phase may need to adapt their controllers. This is because as a consequence of 
the change pods which use RestartPolicy=Always may end up in the Succeeded phase in two scenarios: pod 
deletion and graceful node shutdown.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods_test.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_test.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers_test.go, pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go, pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager_test.go, pkg/kubelet/status/testing/fake_pod_deletion_safety.go, pkg/kubelet/status/testing/mock_pod_status_provider.go

triage.summary: The DeletionTimestamp set by the API Server after a pod deletion does not account for the full termination grace period that was respected during pod termination, causing inconsistencies between the initial deletion event and the final pod deletion time.

evidence.text:
DeletionTimestamp set after grace period is respected does not include grace period time
Dear Kubernetes-Team:

I ran an experiment with an application that does not exit after Kubelet sends an inital SIGTERM signal.
The specified grace-period is respected and the pod is deleted after the grace period finishes.

The deletionTimestamp on the inital delete event seems to include the grace-period, but the deletionTimestamp that is finally updated by the APIServer does not account for the grace-period that was respected. This DeletionTimestamp is also seen when the DeleteFunc is triggered on separate podInformers we have running on our clusters.

I have attached some test results detailing this below; This behavior seems like a bug. The final DeletionTimestamp that is updated by the APIServer should indeed include any grace-period that was respected. (Ideally it should be when the application exits, and not just at the time the user puts in the delete request)


My experiment is as follows:

1) Create a busybox pod with a termination grace period (for example 5 mins)
2) Call delete pod
3) APIServer gets a delete event initiated by the user (k8s-admin) with a deletion timestamp by adding the 5 mins grace period
4) After the grace period ends api server gets another delete event from kubelet (system:node:fargate-ip-19)
5) This delete event from kubelet has grace period of 0 and the DeletionTimestamp set to when user deleted the pod (instead of that time + the respected grace period)

The podspec `busybox.yaml` that is applied: 
```
apiVersion: v1
k

staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/rest/delete.go L110-123 @ aef336d712
OBSERVATION: This code in delete.go manipulates the DeletionTimestamp when a shorter grace period is set by the user (like kubelet). The calculation can result in setting the timestamp earlier than the current time (moving backwards), which may cause the DeletionTimestamp not to include the full grace period that was actually respected, matching the bug description.
if options.GracePeriodSeconds != nil {
	period := int64(*options.GracePeriodSeconds)
	if period >= *objectMeta.GetDeletionGracePeriodSeconds() {
		return false, true, nil
	}
	newDeletionTimestamp := metav1.NewTime(
		objectMeta.GetDeletionTimestamp().Add(-time.Second * time.Duration(*objectMeta.GetDeletionGracePeriodSeconds())).
			Add(time.Second * time.Duration(*options.GracePeriodSeconds)))
	objectMeta.SetDeletionTimestamp(&newDeletionTimestamp)
	objectMeta.SetDeletionGracePeriodSeconds(&period)
	return true, false, nil
}

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the apiserver's deletion handling code in delete.go recalculates and sets the DeletionTimestamp when a shorter grace period is provided (such as by kubelet), potentially moving the timestamp backwards to a time that doesn't include the full grace period that was actually respected. This logic results in the final DeletionTimestamp reflecting the user's initial delete request time instead of the accurate time after the grace period ends.

claims.text: The delete.go code recalculates the DeletionTimestamp by subtracting the original grace period and adding the new shorter grace period, which can set the timestamp backwards before the current time, causing it to not reflect the respected grace period properly.
The store.go code is consistent with the idea that DeletionTimestamp is never set into the future but only moved forward or set to now, meaning moving it backwards is a coding defect.
The Store.Delete method invokes the delete.go logic during deletion, confirming the critical role of this logic in setting the DeletionTimestamp and grace period during pod deletion.

The ticket experimentally confirms that the final DeletionTimestamp after kubectl delete and pod termination reflects the initial deletion request time, not the end of the respected grace period, matching the behavior caused by the delete.go logic.

`"Programmer error, did not report a kubelet_working_pods metric for a value returned by SyncKnownPods" counts=map[{State:sync Orphan:false HasConfig:false Static:false}:1]`.

This suggests a possible bug as it was assumed to do not happen.

ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because pods that were pending start, such as static pods waiting for UID reuse, had their 'pendingUpdate' flag incorrectly cleared. This led the kubelet to not track those pods properly as pending updates, causing the metric 'kubelet_working_pods' not to report them, triggering the 'Programmer error' log during tests. The root cause was improper state management of pod update tracking in the kubelet pod worker logic.

TITLE: cronjob controller: reconsider log verbosity
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We are running Kubernetes 1.25.5 and trying to configure kube-controller-manager to be less verbose when logging.
We run kube-controller-manager as a static pod created by Kubelet and use the following command where we pass `--v=0`:
```
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-controller-manager
    - --feature-gates=EphemeralContainers=true,TopologyAwareHints=true
    - --allocate-node-cidrs=true
    - --authentication-kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/config/controller-manager.conf
    - --authorization-kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/config/controller-manager.conf
    - --cluster-cidr=10.6.0.0/16
    - --configure-cloud-routes=false
    - --kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/config/controller-manager.conf
    - --leader-elect=true
    - --node-monitor-grace-period=120s
    - --root-ca-file=/etc/kubernetes/ssl/ca.pem
    - --service-account-private-key-file=/etc/kubernetes/ssl/signing-key.pem
    - --use-service-account-credentials
    - --v=0
    image: registry.k8s.io/kube-controller-manager:v1.25.5
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    livenessProbe:
      failureThreshold: 3
      httpGet:
        host: 127.0.0.1
        path: /healthz
        po
ROOT CAUSE: The cronjob controller uses a global logging verbosity level of 3 for its event broadcaster, which is independent of the global -v flag passed to kube-controller-manager. As a result, event messages logged with verbosity 4 are always emitted if the global level is 3, ignoring the --v flag. This causes noisy logs even when low verbosity (e.g., --v=0) is requested. The root cause is the broadcaster's logging level is hardcoded and does not depend on the passed verbosity flag.
FIX: kube-controller-manager: increase the global level for broadcaster's logging to 3 so that users can ignore event messages by lowering the logging level. It reduces information noise.
FILES: cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/apps.go, cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/autoscaling.go, cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/core.go, cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/networking.go, pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go, pkg/controller/daemon/daemon_controller.go, pkg/controller/deployment/deployment_controller.go, pkg/controller/disruption/disruption.go, pkg/controller/endpoint/endpoints_controller.go, pkg/controller/endpoint/endpoints_controller_test.go

TITLE: client-go: if an error occurs during request construction, URL() can return a useless result with no indication of an error
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When constructing a `rest.Request`, _e.g._ to stream I/O from a pod:

```
	req := k8s.CoreV1().RESTClient().Post().Resource("pods").Name(podName).Namespace(podNamespace).SubResource("exec")
	req.VersionedParams(&v1.PodExecOptions{
		Command: command,
		Stdin:   false,
		Stdout:  true,
		Stderr:  true,
		TTY:     true,
	}, scheme.ParameterCodec)
	exec, err := remotecommand.NewSPDYExecutor(config, "POST", req.URL())
```

if `req.err` ends up set, `req.URL()` will still return a result without indicating that something went wrong, resulting in a misleading error further down the line. (In my case, I wasn’t providing the correct scheme; the parameters therefore couldn’t be encoded, and the SPDY upgrade failed with an error saying that at least one of stdin, stdout or stderr had to be provided.)

### What did you expect to happen?

Other operations on `rest.Request` fails as appropriate if `req.err` is not `nil`; I would expect `URL()` to do so too. I realise that means a backwards-incompatible change.

Another solution could be to provide a `req.Error()` (same as on the response).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as po
ROOT CAUSE: The code for constructing REST requests accumulates errors internally but the URL() method ignores any existing errors and returns a URL regardless. This leads to users receiving misleading or incorrect URLs without an obvious indication that an earlier error occurred during request construction.
FIX: client-go: add an Error() function on Request
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/request.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/request_test.go

And it seems to only happen when the request is routed to `kube-aggregator`, no similar issues on `kube-apiserv
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the panic was a race condition during the startup of the kube-aggregator's openapi aggregation. diagnosis.root_cause: The bug happens because the code incorrectly wraps and logs the read error using the wrong variable 'err' instead of the actual read error 'errRead' returned by the Read call. As 'err' is nil or unrelated at that point, the wrapped error becomes nil, resulting in logs printing a nil error instead of the real failure reason.

claims.text: The code snippet from staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/remotecommand/websocket.go shows that upon detecting a read error 'errRead', it wraps and sends 'err' to closeAllStreamReaders instead of 'errRead'. 'err' here is nil or unrelated, causing the actual error to be lost and logged as nil.

triage.summary: Compressed pod log files are created with 0644 permissions, making them world-readable, whereas original uncompressed log files have 0600 permissions; this discrepancy is unexpected and should be configurable or inherit original permissions.
code_identifiers: default file permissions for compressed logs

evidence.text:
Compressed pod log files default to 644 permissions
### What happened?

When the pod logs rotate and get compressed, the gzipped file defaults to the permissions of 644. With the directories set to 755 this allows the logs to be world readable at that point.

This appears to be where this issue is happening at - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/logs/container_log_manager.go#L422

### What did you expect to happen?

For the compressed logs to either inherit the original log file permissions (600) or for this file permission to be configurable in the kubelet configuration

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Generate logs & wait until they compress - https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/logging/#basic-logging-in-kubernetes

### What did you expect to happen?

kubectl output logs correctly after the log file is rotated. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Add the config  `containerLogMaxSize: 5Mi` to  `kubelet.yaml`. So kubelet will rotate the log soon.
2.  Build a image with this program
   ```
package main

 import (
        "fmt"
        "time"
 )

 func main() {
        i := 0
        for range time.Tick(10 * time.Microsecond) {
                fmt.Printf("print log to stand out %d\n", i)
                i++
        }
 }
   ```

TITLE: Status manager does not normalize ephemeral container statuses
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

`EphemeralContainerStatuses` is not normalized in 	`normalizeStatus()` in the status manager:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cade1dddd81eba338df85de7b5d17324a87243b5/pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go#L1026-L1043

This does not seem to cause any user facing problem because `EphemeralContainerStatuses` is sorted before passed to the status manager and timestamps are normalized at marshaling to create a patch:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cade1dddd81eba338df85de7b5d17324a87243b5/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L2336

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cade1dddd81eba338df85de7b5d17324a87243b5/pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go#L873

However, an unexpected behavior is caused internally because timestamps are not normalized. If the log verbosity is 3 or larger, the following messages are logged periodically in kubelet when an ephemeral container exists:

```
May 14 20:10:33 kind-control-plane kubelet[720]: I0514 20:10:33.437155 	720 status_manager.go:230] "Syncing all statuses"
May 14 20:10:33 kind-control-plane kubelet[720]: I0514 20:10:33.438512 	720 status_manager.go:984] "Pod status is inconsistent with cache
ROOT CAUSE: The status manager failed to apply normalization logic to EphemeralContainerStatuses when processing pod status updates. This omission caused minor timestamp differences to persist, leading the kubelet to believe pod status was inconsistent and triggering continual unnecessary synchronization attempts.
FIX: normalize ephemeral container statuses
FILES: pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go, pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the temporary file used to store compressed pod logs is explicitly created with file permissions set to 0644 in the function compressLog in pkg/kubelet/logs/container_log_manager.go. This hardcoded permission causes the gzip compressed logs to be world-readable (permission 644) regardless of the original log file permission, which is typically 0600. There is no mechanism to inherit or configure the permission, leading to a potential security exposure where compressed log files are more permissive than intended.

claims.text: The compressLog function in pkg/kubelet/logs/container_log_manager.go creates the temporary compressed log file with a hardcoded permission set to 0644, making the compressed logs world-readable by default.
The issue described in the ticket matches the code behavior where compressed logs have 0644 permissions instead of inheriting the original 0600 permissions or allowing configuration for permissions.

TITLE: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Scheduler should use max(Spec.Resources.Requests, Status.Resources.Requests) instead of Status.AllocatedResources
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Current implementation of in-place pod resize looks at max(Spec.Resources, Status.Resources) which works well when resources are being increased, and works well when resources are being decreased assuming that the decrease request is based on observed lower usage, and the new lowered resources does not exceed current usage.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d86b74b0176c6fa22ba2559ace961fa25c6e98cf/pkg/api/v1/resource/helpers.go#L64-L73

However, a bad actor can game the system by requesting resize to resources lower than current usage, and kubelet grants it not knowing that runtime cannot enforce it, and scheduler may schedule pods to an oversubscribed node. A simple way to avoid this is to use Status.Resources.Requests instead of Status.AllocatedResources.

This also means that containerd and other runtimes need to be at a version that supports the feature so that users get the correct signals (avoid 'forever InProgress')


### What did you expect to happen?

When desired resources are lowered and kubelet admits it and sets status to InProgress, scheduler should schedule new pods against resources that are actually available. Bad actors sho
ROOT CAUSE: The scheduler made scheduling decisions based on the max of requested and status resources without considering that the kubelet might have admitted a decrease below current actual usage. This allowed pods to be resized to resource amounts lower than what the runtime could enforce, causing potential oversubscription and incorrect scheduling.
FIX: ContainerStatus.AllocatedResources is now guarded by a separate feature gate, InPlacePodVerticalSaclingAllocatedStatus

TITLE: Scheduler's default plugin returns an invalid score that is not in the range of [0, 100], resulting in no Pods being scheduled
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Scheduler's default plugin returns an invalid score that is not in the range of [0, 100], resulting in no Pods being scheduled:
```
E1127 19:48:13.221979   66549 schedule_one.go:130] "Error selecting node for pod" err="applying score defaultWeights on Score plugins: plugin \"PodTopologySpread\" returns an invalid score 300, it should in the range of [0, 100] after normalizing" pod="default/test-multi-point-xxxxxxxx"
```

After investigation, I found that there was a bug in the code that built the framework when the scheduler started. When using the plugins declared in the regular extension point to override the plugins declared in the MultiPoint, the traversed variable `enabledSet` will be modified in the following loop:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad9b60e2c9ddb21e8b00cabbe27e639638a0ea88/pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go#L523-L534

This may cause **a same scoring plugin** (e.g. `PodTopologySpread`) **to be loaded multiple times**:
```
f.scorePlugins: []framework.ScorePlugin{(*noderesources.Fit)(0xc000922e10), (*podtopologyspread.PodTopologySpread)(0xc0000ab100), (*podtopologyspread.PodTopologySpread)(0xc0000ab100), (*tai
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the scheduler framework's logic to build plugin lists when merging MultiPoint plugins and regular plugins had a flaw in a loop that led to the same scoring plugin being included multiple times. This caused plugins like PodTopologySpread to execute NormalizeScore multiple times on the same node, producing invalid scores outside the expected [0, 100] range.
FIX: Fixed a regression since 1.24 in the scheduling framework when overriding MultiPoint plugins (e.g. default plugins).
The incorrect loop logic might lead to a plugin being loaded multiple times, consequently preventing any Pod from being scheduled, which is unexpected.
FILES: pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go, pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation scoring plugin mistakenly treats pods with empty resource requests the same as pods requesting only extended resources, which leads to ignoring the pod's requests for native resources like CPU and memory. TITLE: Transition running deleted pods to a terminal phase
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Running pods when deleted are not transitioned to a terminal phase, even when all containers are terminated. Note that, containers are not restarted for deleted pods: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go#L73-L77.

This is problematic for jobs, which as a workaround categorizes all deleted pods (with `deletionTimestamp != nil`) as failed,
but it is still problematic:
- the replacement pod is created too early, leaving two running pods (for the same index) at the same time, which is a problem for some job frameworks. See related Issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115844.
- a pod categorized a failed by the job controller (due to the presence of deletionTimestamp) may end up succeeded if the pod's container completes successfully within the graceful termination period. 
- it blocks a related issue in Jobs: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113855.

The solution might be scoped to pods with finalizers to save a PATCH request to make the transitioning. 

Fixing this issue is planned as part of the Jobs KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3329

### What 
ROOT CAUSE: The kubelet did not transition deleted pods that are still in the Running or Pending phase to a terminal phase (Succeeded or Failed) even when their containers had terminated and would not be restarted due to their RestartPolicy. This caused deleted pods to remain stuck in Running or Pending state indefinitely.
FIX: Give terminal phase correctly to all pods that will not be restarted. 

In particular, assign Failed phase to pods which are deleted while pending. Also, assign a terminal 
phase (Succeeded or Failed, depending on the exit statuses of the pod containers) to pods which
are deleted while running.

This fixes the issue for jobs using pod failure policy (with JobPodFailurePolicy and PodDisruptionConditions 
feature gates enabled) that their pods could get stuck in the pending phase when deleted.

ACTION REQUIRED: Users who maintain controllers which relied on the fact that pods with RestartPolicy=Always
never enter the Succeeded phase may need to adapt their controllers. This is because as a consequence of 
the change pods which use RestartPolicy=Always may end up in the Succeeded phase in two scenarios: pod 
deletion and graceful node shutdown.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods_test.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_test.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers_test.go, pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go, pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager_test.go, pkg/kubelet/status/testing/fake_pod_deletion_safety.go, pkg/kubelet/status/testing/mock_pod_status_provider.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug happens because the kubelet's logic that determines the pod initialization state after a node reboot incorrectly assumes that the pod has already initialized if any main container is running or created. This causes restartable init containers (sidecars), which have restartPolicy "Always", to be skipped or considered already initialized, leading to the pod phase transitioning prematurely from pending to running without running the init containers. This flaw is related to distinguishing container statuses before and after node reboot and handling pod sandbox recreation, as the current logic relies on container states that might be stale or inconsistent across node restarts, allowing regular containers to start before init containers complete.

claims.text: The kubelet code in computeInitContainerActions determines pod initialization based on whether main containers have a created or running status; if so, it treats init containers as already executed, which can be incorrect after node reboot when container statuses might not reflect actual init container executions yet, particularly for restartable init containers.

The ticket describes that pods with init containers having restartPolicy 'Always' lose the pending phase after node reboot and start regular containers before init containers, indicating a defect in pod phase determination and init container lifecycle management after reboot.

TITLE: Jobs create replacement Pods as soon as a Pod is marked for deletion
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When a Pod belonging to a Job is deleted, the job controller creates a replacement pod immediately, even if parallelism is set to 1 and backoffLimit is set to 0.

### What did you expect to happen?

This depends on the use case, but some applications fail when there are more than one pod.

For example, tensorflow fails with:

```
 /job:worker/task:4: Duplicate task registration with task_name=/job:worker/replica:0/task:4
```

This applications will benefit from a delayed Pod creation until the original Pod is marked as Failed/Succeeded.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Job that takes some time to clean up on SIGTERM. You can use `gcr.io/k8s-staging-perf-tests/sleep` with `-termination-grace-period 1m`
2. Delete the pod.
3. Observe that there are two pods running.

While here we do a manual DELETE, it could come as a result of preemption from kube-scheduler or a Node maintenance event, which could be common.

### Anything else we need to know?

IIUC, the existing behavior is similar to that of ReplicaSets and it's the behavior that Jobs had from the beginning.

A comment from an intern
ROOT CAUSE: The job controller initiates creation of replacement pods immediately upon noticing a pod deletion without waiting for the original pod to fully terminate. This premature creation can lead to multiple pods running concurrently when parallelism is set to 1, violating users' expectations and causing application failures. The controller did not implement a mechanism to delay pod creation until the pod state was confirmed as terminated.
FIX: Add implementation for PodRecreationPolicy to wait for creation of pods once the existing ones are fully terminated.
FILES: pkg/controller/controller_utils.go, pkg/controller/controller_utils_test.go, pkg/controller/job/indexed_job_utils.go, pkg/controller/job/indexed_job_utils_test.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go, test/integration/job/job_test.go

TITLE: Job: Pod backoff calculation should not depend on failure policy
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Pod backoff calculation excludes pods that match an `Ignore` rule in the failure policy:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/847f1758748ac357e79094c5e85029a10428e65f/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1365

This could lead to fast retries, overwhelming the control plane, if most failures match an `Ignore` rule. The semantics of `Ignore` is not to count towards the limit, but the backoff should still be respected.


### What did you expect to happen?

Recreations to be throttled.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Job with failure policy that matches every kind of failure.
1. Use a container that always fails

You would observe immediate recreation.

ROOT CAUSE: The backoff delay calculation for recreating pods in a Job controller excluded pods whose failures matched an 'Ignore' rule in the Job's failure policy. While 'Ignore' causes failures not to count towards the limit of retries, the backoff delay should still be applied. Excluding these pods led to the controller immediately recreating pods without respecting backoff delays, causing fast retries and overwhelming the control plane.
FIX: Fix computing backoff delay when using Job pod failure policy, by including in the backoff delay calculation pod failures ignored from the backoffLimit counter

TITLE: CronJob gets stuck when jobs quota is reached
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We (in Booking.com) run CronJobs in Kubernetes clusters with ResourceQuota's defined. When quota for # of jobs is reached we observed that CronJobs:
1. stop scheduling new jobs (because quota is reached),
2. don't clean the old jobs (despite # of jobs > history allows and the fact that it would unblock the CronJob new Jobs). 

The only way to progress is to remove enough Jobs to make room for a new Job in namespace quota. When we do that manually, the CronJob kicks in.

The workaround we found around the internet is to specify `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` for the job template. But it's not ideal as it's not a history-based limit, but a time-based limit, and often you want to have the last N jobs to be around for debugging.

### What did you expect to happen?

When jobs quota is reached and # of cronjob jobs exceeds specified the history limit, these jobs are deleted giving room for new jobs to run.

---
apiVersion: batch/v1

metad
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because when the cronjob controller failed to create a new Job due to hitting the resource quota limit, it aborted the iteration early without performing cleanup of old finished Jobs. This prevented the controller from deleting obsolete Jobs to free quota, causing a deadlock where new Jobs could never be scheduled.
FIX: Fixed an issue where a CronJob could fail to clean up Jobs when the ResourceQuota for Jobs had been reached.

TITLE: A Job might finish with ready!=0, terminating!=0
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When a Job is declared Failed, the running Pods still count as ready.
This causes problems for higher level controllers that use the Failed/Completed conditions to do usage accounting. If the job is marked as finished before all the pods finish, the accounting is inaccurate.

### What did you expect to happen?

A few options (non-necessarily exclusive), in order of my preference:
1. The job not to be declared Completed/Failed until all the Pods have finished. This is possibly a breaking change. As a mitigation, we can use the `FailureTarget` or `SuccessCriteriaMet` conditions to provide early feedback to controllers that a Job is marked for failure.
2. ~Do not count Pods with a deletionTimestamp as ready. (Possibly a breaking change)~
3. ~We just consider ready=0 if setting a finished condition~
4. Continue syncing a Job even after the Failed condition is added, until ready/terminating fields are zero.

Options 2 and 3 don't satisfy the requirement of proper accounting.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Use this Job (note backoffLimit: 0):
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: inde
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug was that the Job was marked as Failed or Completed as soon as failure or success conditions were met, without waiting for all Pods to reach a terminal state. This caused running Pods to still be counted as ready, leading to inaccurate accounting in higher-level controllers that rely on Job conditions.
FIX: Delay setting terminal Job conditions until all pods are terminal.

Additionally, the FailureTarget condition is also added to the Job object in the first Job
status update as soon as the failure conditions are met (backoffLimit is exceeded, maxFailedIndexes, 
or activeDeadlineSeconds is exceeded).

Similarly, the SuccessCriteriaMet condition is added in the first update as soon as the expected number
of pod completions is reached.

Also, introduce the following validation rules for Job status when JobManagedBy is enabled:
1. the count of ready pods is less or equal than active
2. when transitioning to terminal phase for Job, the number of terminating pods is 0
3. terminal Job conditions (Failed and Complete) should be preceded by adding the corresponding interim conditions: FailureTarget and SuccessCriteriaMet
FILES: pkg/apis/batch/validation/validation.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go, pkg/controller/job/success_policy.go, pkg/registry/batch/job/strategy.go, pkg/registry/batch/job/strategy_test.go, test/e2e/apps/job.go, test/e2e/framework/job/wait.go, test/integration/job/job_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The root cause of the bug is that the validation logic for the PodFailurePolicyOnPodConditionsPattern requires the 'status' field to be explicitly set, even though the API type comments indicate a default value of 'True' and documentation suggests the field is optional. This discrepancy causes the validation to reject objects missing the 'status' field, resulting in a required field error when applying the policy without 'status'.

claims.text: The validation function 'validatePodFailurePolicyRuleOnPodConditions' explicitly checks for a non-empty 'status' field and returns a required field error if it is missing, matching the observed error message from the user report.
The API type definition for PodFailurePolicyOnPodConditionsPattern includes a 'Status' field with a comment indicating it defaults to True, suggesting it should be optional and defaulted if omitted.
The documentation and user expectation is that the 'status' field is optional, but the validation enforces it as required, causing a mismatch that breaks API usability.

TITLE: endpoints not configured with MinimizeIPTablesRestore
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

To test out the MinimizeIPTablesRestore feature enabled in 1.27 by default we enabled the setting in 1.26 and discovered that it appears to not configure endpoints properly everytime.
While the version in 1.26 is still alpha I have not found any significant changes, bug reports or backports in the changelog regarding this.

It seems sometimes kube-proxy does not see that the endpoints of a service need to be updated despite the api endpointslice having changed. This typically is not that visible with externalTrafficPolicy Cluster services as some other endpoint still is configured, but in the case of low replica services or externalTrafficPolicy Local services this can lead to service disruption due to the only endpoint on the local node not getting configured while other components see the update correctly and direct traffic there.


For example this two pod deployment both pods ready since hours:

```
$ kubectl -n ns get pods pod1 pod2-o yaml | grep -B 2 Ready

      status: "True"
      type: Ready
--
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:21:19Z"
      status: "True"
      type: ContainersRe
ROOT CAUSE: The bug was caused by a race condition in kube-proxy's iptables mode partial sync logic, where `syncProxyRules` made separate calls to check for pending updates and then apply them. Since the change trackers use their own mutexes independent from the proxier's, a new event could be processed between these calls, leading to inconsistent state and some endpoint updates being missed.
FIX: Fixes a race condition in the iptables mode of kube-proxy in 1.27 and later
that could result in some updates getting lost (e.g., when a service gets a
new endpoint, the rules for the new endpoint might not be added until
much later).

TITLE: Conntrack cleaning happens before network programming endpoints
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Currently kube-proxy efficiently cleans all stale conntrack entries preventing traffic black holing for deleted endpoints, but there can be some corner cases when conntrack cleaning happens before programming the network leaving a small window in which if any packet arrives will back-hole the traffic.

The corner case:
Taking a simple case of load-balancer service backed by a deployment with single replica, on deleting the pod(gracefully), I observed two **OnEndpointSliceUpdate** invocations:
1.  First one with EndpointConditions.Ready as false
2. EndpointSlice was cleared for the pod 

The conntrack flow for this case:
1. After processing the first **OnEndpointSliceUpdate** invocation **EndpointsMap** will still have entries for the pod as endpoint still exists, though not in ready state so proxier won't program deletion of endpoint from the data path. But the endpoint IP will be picked for conntrack cleaning as new endpoint != old endpoint because of the not ready condition.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e915c4288eda15da1724989f3f7dec9f3512d6/pkg/proxy/endpoints.go#L423-L436
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e915c4288e
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the conntrack cleaning logic considers endpoint readiness changes as an indication to clean stale connections before the network datapath has been updated to reflect those changes. This causes a timing window where conntrack entries are cleaned ahead of actual network programming, potentially blackholing traffic.
FIX: Fix stale conntrack flow detection logic
FILES: pkg/proxy/endpoints.go, pkg/proxy/endpoints_test.go, pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go, pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier_test.go, pkg/proxy/types.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs due to an optimization in the Winkernel proxier's updateLoadBalancer function, which uses a cached hash of endpoints to avoid redundant HNS ModifyLoadBalancer calls. If the cache key (built from protocol, ports, VIP, and endpoints hash) incorrectly matches a previous load balancer state that is actually stale or if the cache is not properly invalidated after pod scaling, the proxier skips calling HNS to update the load balancer endpoints. This results in the HNS load balancer policy still reflecting the old endpoints even though KubeProxy attempted an update, leading to stale endpoint lists observed in HNS after scaling pods.

claims.text: The updateLoadBalancer function builds a hash of endpoints and uses it as a cache key to decide whether to call HNS UpdateLoadBalancer or skip it if an identical load balancer configuration is already cached.

If the cache key matches a previous load balancer with an out-of-date endpoint list (e.g., after scaling pods but hash or cache not properly updated), the function returns early, skipping the HNS update call, leading to stale endpoint lists in HNS.

The problem described in the ticket matches this caching optimization causing the HNS load balancer policy endpoints to not reflect updated pod endpoints after scaling, causing kube-proxy to fail the load balancer update.

TITLE: Transient Driver Registration on the CSINode can Result in Missed NodeUnstageVolume RPCs During Pod Migration
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

In `unmountDetachDevices` (see [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/03126c5465879491be33d5064e6f6f1c4ff2a276/pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/reconciler/reconciler_common.go#L279-L316)) we have the following code that will ultimately dispatch `NodeUnstageVolume` RPCs to the underlying CSI plugin.

Here is a pseudo-code representation of the current logic:

```
function unmountDetachDevices
	for all unmounted volumes in ASoW
		if volume not in DSoW &&
		   not operation pending on volume
			if device is mounted globally or
			   device is mounted uncertain
				Case A:
				unmount device
				(this will kick off the NodeUnstageVolume RPC; we want to be here)
			else
				Case B:
				just remove volume from ASoW
				(general badness since we don't issue a NodeUnstageVolume RPC)
```

In our testbeds, we have observed a number of occurrences where we fall into `Case B` when the CSI Node plugin for a particular driver is being bounced, which leads to the volumemanager failing to dispatch the `NodeUnstageVolume` RPC. If the pod migrates to another node, this will leave behind a Zombie LUN in our testbeds (we're using iSCSI).

A Zombie LUN can and often does resu
ROOT CAUSE: The CSI attacher treats the absence of the CSI driver during a NodeStageVolume call as a final error, transitioning volume devices from uncertain to unmounted state prematurely. This causes unmountDetachDevices logic to skip issuing NodeUnstageVolume RPCs, potentially leaving volumes in a zombie state. The root cause is misclassification of a missing CSI driver error as final rather than transient, leading to incorrect device state transitions and missed cleanup calls.
FIX: Retry NodeStageVolume calls if CSI node driver is not running

claims.text: The expandOnPlugin function, responsible for node-side volume expansion, does not handle NotSupported errors from the volume plugin's NodeExpand operation by marking the expansion as successful, causing persistent error conditions.

Because the new expandOnPlugin function lacks this workaround, CSI drivers that do not implement NodeExpandVolume cause NodeResizeError to remain set indefinitely even though the volume expansion actually succeeded at the controller level and the volume is usable.

TITLE: Graceful node shutdown doesn't wait for volume teardown
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We have observed that after a node is preempted, pods using persistent volumes take 6+ minutes to restart. This happens when a volume was not able to be cleanly unmounted (indicated by updating `Node.Status.VolumesInUse`), which causes the Attach/Detach controller (in kube-controller-manager) to wait for 6 minutes before issuing a force detach. In addition to a long pod restart period, an unclean mount could also cause data corruption.

From the logs we've observed the following non-ideal behaviors, which I think reduces to the same issue that we only check for containers' being terminated and not their volumes.

1. The CSI driver running on the node gets terminated before the workload's volumes get unmounted. This causes unmount to fail. In our case, the CSI driver is part of the `system-node-critical" class, but since we don't wait for volumes to be unmounted, we move on to shutting down the critical pods.

3. The OS gets shutdown before volume teardown is completed, even if there is still time left in the `shutdownGracePeriod`. In our case, the `shutdownGracePeriod` is set to 30 seconds, however we see that the node got shutdown in 10 seconds, even wh
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that during node shutdown, the shutdown manager checks only for pod termination to proceed without ensuring that volumes used by these pods are successfully unmounted. Since volume teardown only starts after containers have stopped, there is a race condition where the CSI driver may be terminated or the OS may shut down before volumes are fully detached, leading to unclean unmounts and prolonged pod restarts.
FIX: Node shutdown controller now makes a best effort to wait for CSI Drivers to complete the volume teardown process according to the pod priority groups.

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the Kubelet's node volume expansion logic does not properly clear the NodeResizePending condition from the PVC's AllocatedResourceStatuses after a successful NodeExpandVolume call. This is likely due to failure or missing calls to util.MarkFSResizeFinished in the legacyCallNodeExpandOnPlugin method that should update the PVC status to remove NodeResizePending. Consequently, the PVC status incorrectly indicates resize is still pending despite the successful node-side expansion, causing a persistent NodeResizePending condition. The version skew between control plane and node exacerbates this mismatch, as node logs show a benign but misleading NodeExpandVolume failure error that does not trigger clearing the condition properly.

claims.text: The NodeResizePending condition is set by markForPendingNodeExpansion after controller volume expansion to mark that filesystem resize is still required on the node.
After node expansion, legacyCallNodeExpandOnPlugin calls util.MarkFSResizeFinished to update the PVC status and clear NodeResizePending; if this update fails, NodeResizePending remains stuck.

The bug report shows NodeResizePending condition persists despite NodeExpandVolume success and node logs showing a failure error that is benign, indicative of the node expansion clearing logic not completing successfully.

The issue occurs with control plane and node version skew, aggravating the stale status because the Kubelet's logic expects coordination in clearing NodeResizePending which does not happen correctly under version skew.

SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

1. But the endpoint IP will be picked for conntrack cleaning as new endpoint != old endpoint because of the not ready condition.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e915c4288e

TITLE: Scheduler will run into race conditions on large scale clusters
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

A race condition will happen in the follow case:

1. pod1 is assigned to a node, scheduler cache is updated with the assignment, bind operation issued to apiserver.

1. if the apiserver is under huge pressure, bind takes more than 30s, scheduler expires the cached pod-to-node assignment.

1. bind eventually succeeds, but because the apiserver is under huge pressure, the pod update with the node name takes a long time to propagate to the scheduler.

1. because the pod update took a long time to propagate and the cache entry expired, the scheduler is not aware that the assignment actually happened, and so it had no problem assigning a second pod to the same node that would otherwise not fit if the scheduler was aware that the fi
ROOT CAUSE: The scheduler's cache entries for pod-to-node assignments expire after a fixed 30-second timeout. When the API server is under heavy load and the bind operation takes longer than 30s, the cache prematurely removes the assignment. This causes the scheduler to lose track of the actual binding state, leading it to incorrectly schedule another pod onto the same node, resulting in race conditions on large clusters.

SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Scheduler's default plugin returns an invalid score that is not in the range of [0, 100], resulting in no Pods being scheduled:

After investigation, I found that there was a bug in the code that built the framework when the scheduler started. When using the plugins declared in the regular extension point to override the plugins declared in the MultiPoint, the traversed variable `enabledSet` will be modified in the following loop:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad9b60e2c9ddb21e8b00cabbe27e639638a0ea88/pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go#L523-L534

This may cause **a same scoring plugin** (e.g. `PodTopologySpread`) **to be loaded multiple times**:
```
f.scorePlugins: []framework.ScorePlugin{(*noderesources.Fit)(0xc000922e10), (*podtopologyspread.PodTopologySpread)(0xc0000ab100), (*podtopologyspread.PodTopologySpread)(0xc0000ab100), (*tai
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the scheduler framework's logic to build plugin lists when merging MultiPoint plugins and regular plugins had a flaw in a loop that led to the same scoring plugin being included multiple times. This caused plugins like PodTopologySpread to execute NormalizeScore multiple times on the same node, producing invalid scores outside the expected [0, 100] range.
FIX: Fixed a regression since 1.24 in the scheduling framework when overriding MultiPoint plugins (e.g. default plugins).

triage.summary: Job controller incorrectly creates multiple pods for a job with parallelism and completions set to 1 due to race condition in updating Job.status.uncountedTerminatedPods and removing pod finalizers during the same reconcile loop, leading to miscounting succeeded pods especially in busy clusters with delayed watch events.

evidence.text:
Job controller's race condition - Pod finalizer removal and job uncounted status update should work in separate reconcile
### What happened?

Job controller accidentally created two pods even if the Job spec specifies in a busy cluster:

```
  parallelism: 1
  completions: 1
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 86400
  backoffLimit: 0
```

This is happening because when job controller is calculating the succeed pods, it's taking three inputs ([here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L892)):

1. The completion count from `Job.status.succeeded`
2. The existing succeed pods (if the finalizer is still present)
3. The uncounted completion count from `Job.status.uncountedTerminatedPods`

Due to the current implementation where the job controller is refreshing both (2) and (3) in the same reconcile/sync process:

> https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1165-L1167

The job controller may miscount the succeeded pods when the watch event for (3) hasn't reach the controller. A delayed watch event is fairly likely to happened in a busy cluster.

### What did you expect to happen?

The better implementation should be handling the refreshing of (2) and (3) in separate reconcile process:

(1) in the 1st reconcile, job controller should only refresh `Job.status.uncountedTerminatedPods` while preserving the finalizers on the pods
(2) in the 2nd reconcile which is triggered by (1), job controller is safe to remove the finalizers from pods

TITLE: Job controller reports the count of ready pods with unnecessary delay
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When Job controller is deleting pods the counter in the status.ready field does not reflect this properly (there is a delay until the cache is refreshed). This affects the scenarios of terminating job, suspended job, and excess pods deleted.

### What did you expect to happen?

The ready field is updated as soon as the delete requests are sent successfully, in sync with the status.active field.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. To see this you can scale down a job, use the following yaml:
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: simple-job
spec:
  completions: 2
  parallelism: 2
  completionMode: Indexed
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: 'worker'
        image: python
        command:
        - python3
        - -c
        - |
          import time
          time.sleep(300)
```

2. Watch for the job updates with the following watcher:
```
kubectl get jobs -w --output-watch-events -ocustom-columns=EVENT:.type,NAME:.object.metadata.name,READY:.object.status.ready,ACTIVE:.object.status.active,TERMINATING:.object.status.terminat
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the Job controller counts ready pods only among the currently active pods during deletion, but since the number of active pods updates asynchronously and may decrease after the count was made, the ready pod count does not get updated promptly to reflect pods that are terminating or deleted. This lag causes stale ready counts until the cache refreshes.
FIX: Now the .status.ready field is tracked faster when active Pods are deleted, specifically when Job is failed, gets suspended or has too many active pods
FILES: pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go

TITLE: The event handlers of job controller are slow
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The event handlers in job controller are much slower than other controllers. It can cause the ring buffer in the processorListener to grow unbounded when the job churn is high enough.
The processing logic in the job controller events handler appears to be more complicated than other controllers. e.g. in [updateJob](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dbc2b0a5c7acc349ea71a14e49913661eaf708d2/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L464-L504), it invokes function `cleanupPodFinalizers` that lists the pods matching some selectors and the enqueue them to another queue. Similarly in [deleteJob](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dbc2b0a5c7acc349ea71a14e49913661eaf708d2/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L508-L524).

I added some instrumenting code to understand the latency of each event handler.
For job controller P99:
job add event handler: 0.080 ms
job update event handler: 3.075 ms
job delete event handler: 3.076 ms
pod add event handler: 0.136 ms
pod update event handler: 0.709 ms
pod delete event handler: 0.405 ms

For ttl-after-completion controller P99:
job add event handler: 0.0065 ms
job update event handler: 0.024 ms

T
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the slowness is that the job controller's event handlers perform complex and expensive operations directly within the event handler methods, such as listing pods and enqueuing them, instead of deferring such processing to the controller's main reconcile loop. This design leads to high latency and potential buildup of events, especially under high job churn.
FIX: Improve performance of the job controller when handling job update events.
FILES: pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go

TITLE: Jobs create replacement Pods as soon as a Pod is marked for deletion
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When a Pod belonging to a Job is deleted, the job controller creates a replacement pod immediately, even if parallelism is set to 1 and backoffLimit is set to 0.

### What did you expect to happen?

This depends on the use case, but some applications fail when there are more than one pod.

For example, tensorflow fails with:

```
 /job:worker/task:4: Duplicate task registration with task_name=/job:worker/replica:0/task:4
```

This applications will benefit from a delayed Pod creation until the original Pod is marked as Failed/Succeeded.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Job that takes some time to clean up on SIGTERM. You can use `gcr.io/k8s-staging-perf-tests/sleep` with `-termination-grace-period 1m`
2. Delete the pod.
3. Observe that there are two pods running.

While here we do a manual DELETE, it could come as a result of preemption from kube-scheduler or a Node maintenance event, which could be common.

### Anything else we need to know?

IIUC, the existing behavior is similar to that of ReplicaSets and it's the behavior that Jobs had from the beginning.

A comment from an intern
ROOT CAUSE: The job controller initiates creation of replacement pods immediately upon noticing a pod deletion without waiting for the original pod to fully terminate. This premature creation can lead to multiple pods running concurrently when parallelism is set to 1, violating users' expectations and causing application failures. The controller did not implement a mechanism to delay pod creation until the pod state was confirmed as terminated.
FIX: Add implementation for PodRecreationPolicy to wait for creation of pods once the existing ones are fully terminated.

TITLE: A Job might finish with ready!=0, terminating!=0
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When a Job is declared Failed, the running Pods still count as ready.
This causes problems for higher level controllers that use the Failed/Completed conditions to do usage accounting. If the job is marked as finished before all the pods finish, the accounting is inaccurate.

### What did you expect to happen?

A few options (non-necessarily exclusive), in order of my preference:
1. The job not to be declared Completed/Failed until all the Pods have finished. This is possibly a breaking change. As a mitigation, we can use the `FailureTarget` or `SuccessCriteriaMet` conditions to provide early feedback to controllers that a Job is marked for failure.
2. ~Do not count Pods with a deletionTimestamp as ready. (Possibly a breaking change)~
3. ~We just consider ready=0 if setting a finished condition~
4. Continue syncing a Job even after the Failed condition is added, until ready/terminating fields are zero.

Options 2 and 3 don't satisfy the requirement of proper accounting.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Use this Job (note backoffLimit: 0):
```yaml

kind: Job
metadata:
  name: inde
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug was that the Job was marked as Failed or Completed as soon as failure or success conditions were met, without waiting for all Pods to reach a terminal state. This caused running Pods to still be counted as ready, leading to inaccurate accounting in higher-level controllers that rely on Job conditions.
FIX: Delay setting terminal Job conditions until all pods are terminal.

Additionally, the FailureTarget condition is also added to the Job object in the first Job
status update as soon as the failure conditions are met (backoffLimit is exceeded, maxFailedIndexes, 
or activeDeadlineSeconds is exceeded).

Similarly, the SuccessCriteriaMet condition is added in the first update as soon as the expected number
of pod completions is reached.

1. the count of ready pods is less or equal than active

When Job controller is terminating and deletes all pods the counter in the `status.terminating` field does not reflect this properly. 

### What did you expect to happen?

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Run the Job:

spec:

ROOT CAUSE: The Job controller failed to increment the counter for terminating pods when it actively deletes pods during job termination, particularly for failed jobs. This caused the .status.terminating field to not reflect terminating pods accurately, leading to delayed or incorrect status updates.
FIX: .status.terminating field now gets tracked faster when active Pods are deleted, specifically when Job is failed, gets suspended or has too many active pods
FILES: pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go, test/integration/job/job_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the Job controller updates both the job status's uncountedTerminatedPods and removes pod finalizers within the same reconcile loop. When the event for updating uncountedTerminatedPods is delayed under high load, the controller miscounts succeeded pods, leading it to prematurely create replacement pods even if the specified completions and parallelism should prevent this. The lack of separation between these two operations causes a race where pod counting and finalizer removal steps interfere, causing the controller state to be temporarily inconsistent.

claims.text: The ticket explains that the Job controller calculates succeeded pods count from jobStatus.succeeded, existing succeed pods (pods with finalizers), and jobStatus.uncountedTerminatedPods, updating both finalizer removal and uncountedTerminatedPods in one reconcile loop, which can lead to miscounting when the watch event for uncountedTerminatedPods is delayed.

The key function 'trackJobStatusAndRemoveFinalizers' in job_controller.go performs both removal of pod finalizers and updates to uncountedTerminatedPods in the same reconcile, causing potential race conditions as described in the ticket.

Delayed watch events in busy clusters are likely, making it probable that job status updates lag behind pod finalizer removals, causing stale or miscounted pod completion counts and triggering extra pod creation.

Past incidents show that Job controller's pod counting and status updates can experience delays or inconsistencies under concurrent updates, reinforcing that delayed state propagation causes inaccurate pod counting and status, as seen in kb-125185 and kb-125089 related to delayed updates of pod counts in job status.

TITLE: Kubelet panic when allocates device for pods.
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

It is suspected to be a concurrent bug of kubelet.

When we delete the last pod that requires GPU on the node and create two or more pods that require GPU at the same time, kubelet may panic on `allocateContainerResources` as following.

I think it's a concurrency issue.

1. Create a pod with GPU request, then kubelet will allocate resource for it. Kubelet try call device plugin to choose preferred device for it. **It will unlock the mutex!.** https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L984-L1006
2. Then we delete the last pod that requires GPU.
3. Create the second pod with GPU request, kubelet will allocate resource for it also. Kubelet will call `UpdateAllocatedDevices` to recalculate device (delete allocated device if pod deleted). It will update the **allocatedDevices** map of ManagerImpl, because of mutex is unlock by step 1. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L519-L543
4.  Kubelet continues with the first pod. If **allocatedDevices** has changed and GPU device is nil, kubelet will panic in the closure allocateRemainingFrom.

```
Jul 25 1
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is a concurrency race in kubelet's device manager when allocating GPU devices to pods. The mutex guarding the allocated devices map is unlocked while calling out to device plugins, allowing concurrent updates and leading to inconsistent or nil map values. This causes the allocation function to panic due to nil map assignments when multiple GPU-using pods are created or deleted concurrently.
FIX: Fix kubelet panic when allocate resource for pod.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go, pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager_test.go
