diagnosis.root_cause: The kubelet podresources API List endpoint fetches pods via podsProvider.GetPods(), which returns all pods including terminated ones, without filtering them out. Because CPU and memory resource managers rely on this full pod list without syncing allocations or filtering active pods only (unlike device resource managers which perform explicit syncing), the API reports stale resource data for terminated pods. This discrepancy between the podresources API pod list and the resource managers' active pods list causes terminated pods' resources to be incorrectly reported.

claims.text: The List method in the podresources API server retrieves pods through p.podsProvider.GetPods(), which returns pods irrespective of their termination status, causing the API to report resources for terminated pods.
The podManager's GetPods method returns all pods in podByUID map without filtering out terminated pods, which leads to the podresources List method reporting resources for terminated pods.

The podresources API differs from resource managers by using all pods known through podManager, while the resource managers use only active pods, leading to stale data inclusion for CPU and memory resources.

triage.summary: In kube-proxy's nftables proxy-mode, when a LoadBalancer Service with externalTrafficPolicy:Local and an ExternalIP is used, traffic from pods to the external IP is incorrectly dropped due to iptables rules created that blackhole this traffic. Expected behavior is to allow load balancing to target Service endpoints even when no local endpoints are present on the node.

evidence.text:
kube-proxy: externalTrafficPolicy:Local and proxy-mode=nftables blackholes pods traffic to external IPs
### What happened?

When using kube-proxy on nftables mode and specify a `LoadBalancer` Service with `externalTrafficPolicy:Local` that has an ExternalIP assigned, kube-proxy will create an entry in the kube-proxy ip nftable that will drop traffic to that external IP, like:

```
        map no-endpoint-services {
                type ipv4_addr . inet_proto . inet_service : verdict
                comment "vmap to drop or reject packets to services with no endpoints"
                elements = { 
                             10.88.1.2 . tcp . 80 comment "sys-ingress-priv/internal-ingress-controller-v2:web" : drop,
```

As a result, any pod on the host cannot send traffic to the external IP of the LoadBalancer.

### What did you expect to happen?

On nodes where no workload is present, traffic should not be dropped but load balanced by kube proxy to the target Service endpoints.
This will also bring consistency with how other modes work, as this issue was addressed both for ipvs (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/93456)
and iptables (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/77523) modes.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run kube-proxy on nftables mode and try hitting a `LoadBalancer` Service `ExternalIP` from within a pod running in a node that does not have ready endpoints of the target service

### Anything else we need to know?

@kubernetes/sig-network-bugs
Simmilar to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/7

TITLE:  kube-proxy: traffic to healthcheck host ports is dropped because of iptables rule order
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We are running self managed Kubernetes clusters on GCP and use Services of `type: LoadBalancer` with both public and private `EXTERNAL-IP`s to create load balancers for our clusters. Since upgrading kube-proxy to 1.26.3 (from 1.25.5) we saw that all healthchecks from GCP started to fail and traffic is now blindly load balanced across all nodes, which broke Services with
`externalTrafficPolicy` set to `Local`.
The issue seems to be introduced with this change: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/108460
Here, `KUBE-IPVS-IPS` ipset is introduced and is used in iptables on chain `KUBE-IPVS-FILTER` as:
```
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-LOAD-BALANCER dst,dst -j RETURN
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-CLUSTER-IP dst,dst -j RETURN                                                                                                                                           
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-EXTERNAL-IP dst,dst -j RETURN
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m conntrack --ctstate NEW -m set --match-set KUBE-IPVS-IPS dst -j REJECT --reject-with icmp-port-unreachable 
```
`KUBE-IPVS-IPS` seems to include external IPs (as al
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug is that the iptables rule ordering in the KUBE-IPVS-FILTER chain wrongly rejected packets to healthCheckNodePorts on loadBalancer IPs, due to a restrictive rule introduced to reject new connections to IPVS IPs except for known service IPs. This rule blocked healthcheck traffic from GCP to the node ports for health checking, causing probes to fail. The healthCheckNodePort accept rule was missing in the iptables filter chain prior to the rejecting rule, causing legitimate healthcheck traffic to be dropped.
FIX: fixes 1.26 regression in kube-proxy ipvs accepting healthCheckNodePorts on the loadBalancerIP
FILES: pkg/proxy/ipvs/proxier.go

TITLE: Can't restrict access from K8s nodes with loadBalancerSourceRanges for proxy-mode=ipvs
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When using loadBalancerSourceRanges to allow access only from CIDRs outside the cluster segment, access from the K8s nodes (or pods with hostNetwork:true) should be rejected, but for proxy-mode=ipvs it works.



### What did you expect to happen?

Access from K8s nodes should be rejected in the same way as for proxy-mode=iptables

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Define a service with loadBalancerSourceRanges that allows access from a cidr outside the cluster, e.g.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: alpine
spec:
  loadBalancerSourceRanges:
#  - "192.168.1.0/24"
  - "192.168.2.0/24"
#  - "fd00::c0a8:100/120"
  - "fd00::c0a8:200/120"
  ipFamilyPolicy: RequireDualStack
  selector:
    app: alpine
  type: LoadBalancer
  allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false
  ports:
  - port: 5001
    name: nc
```
The K8s nodes have addresses on 192.168.1.0/24 and fd00::c0a8:100/120.

Make sure a loadBalancerIP is assigned (in this example 10.0.0.0/32) and try to access it from a K8s node:
```
# With proxy.mode=ipvs
> nc 10.0.0.0:5001
alpine-f6c8bd7db-zljnl    # (works)
# With proxy.mod
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the IPVS proxier was not correctly identifying the node ID when applying loadBalancerSourceRanges filtering, causing it to allow access from Kubernetes nodes that should have been rejected. Without the correct node ID, IPVS could not properly enforce source range restrictions, unlike iptables mode which handled them correctly.
FIX: Hardening LB SourceRanges filtering for IPVS proxier
FILES: pkg/proxy/ipvs/proxier.go, pkg/proxy/ipvs/proxier_test.go

TITLE: endpoints not configured with MinimizeIPTablesRestore
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

To test out the MinimizeIPTablesRestore feature enabled in 1.27 by default we enabled the setting in 1.26 and discovered that it appears to not configure endpoints properly everytime.
While the version in 1.26 is still alpha I have not found any significant changes, bug reports or backports in the changelog regarding this.

It seems sometimes kube-proxy does not see that the endpoints of a service need to be updated despite the api endpointslice having changed. This typically is not that visible with externalTrafficPolicy Cluster services as some other endpoint still is configured, but in the case of low replica services or externalTrafficPolicy Local services this can lead to service disruption due to the only endpoint on the local node not getting configured while other components see the update correctly and direct traffic there.


For example this two pod deployment both pods ready since hours:

```
$ kubectl -n ns get pods pod1 pod2-o yaml | grep -B 2 Ready
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:21:19Z"
      status: "True"
      type: Ready
--
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:21:19Z"
      status: "True"
      type: ContainersRe
ROOT CAUSE: The bug was caused by a race condition in kube-proxy's iptables mode partial sync logic, where `syncProxyRules` made separate calls to check for pending updates and then apply them. diagnosis.root_cause: The kube-proxy nftables proxier unconditionally adds rules in the serviceEndpointsCheckChain that drop traffic to ExternalIPs with no local endpoints, without correctly handling traffic originating from pods on nodes without endpoints. Because the nftables filter output chain has a higher priority drop rule that drops packets to these "no endpoint services" before DNAT rules can reroute traffic to remote endpoints, pods on nodes without local endpoints cannot reach the Service via the ExternalIP. Attempts to use original destination IP from conntrack for matching fail due to nftables limitations on variable-sized data usage in maps, preventing a fix similar to other proxy modes. This causes traffic blackholing, unlike iptables or ipvs modes that handle this case properly by DNATing traffic to endpoints in other nodes.

claims.text: The proxier sets up a noEndPoints drop map and adds a rule to drop packets to services with no endpoints unconditionally in the nftables filter output chain.

Traffic originating within the cluster destined for ExternalIP is dropped before the DNAT rule that would redirect it to cluster endpoints is applied, due to nftables rule ordering and priorities (-110 for filter-output chain being before DNAT).

An attempt to fix this by matching using original destination IP and port via conntrack failed because nftables does not support using ct original proto-dst in concat expressions with vmap, making the intended fix impossible.
This bug reproduces the previously known issue for iptables and ipvs modes, which were fixed by properly handling the no endpoint case and not dropping traffic but redirecting it.

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs due to a race condition between the asynchronous goroutine readDemuxLoop and the stream creation inside streamer.stream. This leads to messages received for unknown stream IDs and triggers the "Unknown stream id x, discarding message" error.

When readDemuxLoop reads messages with a stream ID not yet known (not created), it logs the error 'Unknown stream id x, discarding message' indicating a race between stream creation and message handling.
The ticket explicitly states the suspected root cause is a race between the stream and readDemuxLoop goroutines, where readDemuxLoop may request a stream before it exists.

SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

For example:
- node with 96 cores
- cpu limit 94
- `runtime.NumCPU()` returns `48`

This results in a CPU maximum of 10000 since the range is from [1, 10000]:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container_windows.go#L82..L91

```go
	limit := int64(94 * 1000)
	numCPU := 48
	fmt.Println(((10000 * limit) / int64(numCPU) / 1000))


```

Our initial goal for this was to limit a process to not use all available CPU and therefore render the node uncontrollable. 

### What did you expect to happen?

A CPU maximum of `9791` instead of `10000` for that specific case. For the calculation, it should use the CPU count for all available processor groups instead of just the current one. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Launch a node with a lot of CPUs, for example [a Azure Standard_D96a_v4](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azur
ROOT CAUSE: The bug was caused because the code incorrectly used `runtime.NumCPU()` to determine the number of logical CPUs on Windows nodes. This function only returns the number of processors in the current processor group and does not aggregate CPU counts across multiple processor groups, leading to an underestimated CPU count when nodes have more than 64 logical processors. This incorrect CPU count causes the CPU maximum calculation to be incorrect for such nodes.

diagnosis.root_cause: The PreferAlignByUncoreCache CPU manager policy implementation uses integer division to calculate needed CPU cores from requested CPUs, which truncates when an odd number of CPUs is requested. This causes the partial UncoreCache allocation to fail for odd CPU counts less than a full cache size, falling back to non-aligned CPU assignment and thus not honoring the alignment preference.

claims.text: The takePartialUncore method uses integer division (numCPUsNeeded / CPUsPerCore) which rounds down and causes allocation to not match requested odd number of CPUs, leading to the observed allocation failure for 7 CPUs.

Due to the above integer division rounding, requests for odd number of CPUs less than a full UncoreCache fall through alignment allocation and revert to fallback allocation that is not aligned, as described in the ticket and code behavior.

The policy enforces full-core alignment implicitly by dividing requested CPUs by CPUsPerCore, which disallows odd CPU count allocation under SMT enabled scenarios without the full-pcpus-only option being enabled.

TITLE: kubelet: Evicted and force deleted pods get their full termination grace period when they should not
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When pods are evicted, i.e. with a hard eviction, the grace period is intended to be `0s` (i.e. do not respect the pod's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`). 

However, currently, evicted pods receive their full termination grace period seconds.

### What did you expect to happen?

The pod is evicted immediately and the termination grace period is not respected 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy the following pod which has an ephemeral storage limit of 5Mi and uses `dd` to fill the disk

```
kind: Pod
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: evictdiskpod
  labels:
    pod: evictdiskpod
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60
  containers:
  - name: busybox
    image: k8s.gcr.io/e2e-test-images/nginx:1.14-2
    resources:
      limits:
        ephemeral-storage: 5Mi
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
      - |
        _term() {
            echo "Caught SIGTERM signal!"
            while true; do sleep 5; done
        }
        trap _term SIGTERM
        sleep 10
        dd if=/dev/zero of=file bs=1M count=10
        echo 'write done'
        while true; do sleep 5; done
```

2
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because a grace period override of 0 was used during eviction to force immediate pod termination, but the pod worker logic interpreted a zero override as no override and used the pod's full configured grace period. This caused evicted and force deleted pods to respect their full termination grace period instead of being terminated immediately. To enforce immediate eviction, a grace period override of 1 second must be used instead of zero.
FIX: Fixes a bug where hard evictions due to resource pressure would let the pod have the full termination grace period, instead of shutting down instantly. This bug also affected force deleted pods. Both cases now get a termination grace period of 1 second.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go, pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager_test.go, pkg/kubelet/eviction/helpers_test.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the KillPodOptions struct, which includes an unmarshalable channel field (CompletedCh), is logged directly using the default JSON marshaler. The presence of the channel field causes the JSON marshaler to error with "unsupported type: chan<- struct {}", resulting in the internal error message seen in the log. The code does not implement a custom marshaler for KillPodOptions at the logging site, so the logging system attempts to marshal the channel field, which is inherently unsupported by JSON marshaling in Go.

claims.text: The KillPodOptions struct contains a channel field CompletedCh which cannot be JSON marshaled and causes marshaling errors when logged directly.
The code logs killPodOptions directly in pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go, which includes the channel field, causing the internal marshal error seen in the ticket logs.

TITLE: DaemonSet fails to scale down during the rolling update when `maxUnavailable=0`
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I have a daemonset with the rolling update strategy. I have `maxSurge` parameter set to a non zero value [which means](https://github.com/openshift/kubernetes/blob/cb4b47e5ddfbaf7844237b2e2eb2b0acfed5f1b5/pkg/apis/apps/validation/validation.go#L394-L402) that the `maxUnavailable` parameter is set to `0`. When I replace the toleration in the daemonset's template spec from the one which helped me to be scheduled on the master node into any other toleration, I see the new pods still trying to be scheduled on the master nodes. The old pods from the tolerated nodes can be lucky enough to be recreated but only if they go before any pod from the intolerable node.

```
$ kubectl -n openshift-dns get ds dns-default -o yaml | yq .spec.updateStrategy
rollingUpdate:
  maxSurge: 10%
  maxUnavailable: 0
type: RollingUpdate

$ kubectl -n openshift-dns get ds dns-default -o yaml | yq .spec.template.spec.tolerations
- key: node-role.kubernetes.io/master
  operator: Exists
  
$ kubectl -n openshift-dns get pods  -o wide | grep dns-default
dns-default-6bfmf     2/2     Running   0          119m    10.129.0.40   ci-ln-sb5ply2-72292-qlhc8-master-2         <none>     
ROOT CAUSE: The daemonset rolling update logic included all nodes with existing pods for updating regardless of whether the new daemonset's tolerations matched the nodes' taints. This caused new pods to be scheduled on intolerable nodes and the old pods on tolerable nodes not to be deleted, leading to the update being stuck when maxUnavailable was 0.
FIX: Revised the logic for DaemonSet rolling update to exclude nodes if scheduling constraints are not met.
This eliminates the problem of rolling updates to a DaemonSet getting stuck around tolerations.
FILES: pkg/controller/daemon/update.go, pkg/controller/daemon/update_test.go, test/integration/daemonset/daemonset_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the StatefulSet controller's scale-down logic with podManagementPolicy=OrderedReady and minReadySeconds blocks termination of pods until the first unhealthy pod becomes available (ready and satisfies minReadySeconds). If a pod is ready but not yet available due to minReadySeconds, the controller waits and only retries scaling when a full controller manager resync happens, causing scale-down to stall. claims.text: The processCondemned function blocks scaling down pods if the first unhealthy pod is not running, ready, and available, causing delay in terminating pods during scale-down with OrderedReady policy and minReadySeconds.

The StatefulSet controller enqueues statefulsets for reprocessing after minReadySeconds when pods transition from not ready to ready, but this enqueueing leads to delayed scaling-down until a full resync or availability condition is met.

The syncStatefulSet function also requeues the StatefulSet if available replicas do not match desired replicas under minReadySeconds, reinforcing the delay in scale-down until availability conditions are met or controller resync occurs.

TITLE: Scheduling Pods with dynamic resources and using the Pod `.spec.nodeName` field fails
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The combination of using the Pod spec nodeName field with the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin (currently feature-gated) doesn't work. No surprise really as the nodeName field effective bypasses the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin running, and something rather clever would need to be invented to make things to work. But this is still a bit of a regression compared to the old device plugin model which doesn't have a similar limitation.  @pohly as the author of the dynamic resources feature can explain what could maybe be created to fix this.

Granted, forcing scheduling even with a device plugin resource may or may not succeed at the node level depending on the availability of said plugin resources at the node, but with dynamic resources the failure seems to be currently guaranteed.

The use-case for this is such that the Kubernetes scheduler is effectively being preceded by some other scheduler which runs earlier (say, some HPC framework) which is giving the Pods the node names and somehow knows that there will be enough resources, and then the workloads ought to land in the specified node and the container related work is then handled normally from t

TITLE: Transition running deleted pods to a terminal phase
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Running pods when deleted are not transitioned to a terminal phase, even when all containers are terminated. Note that, containers are not restarted for deleted pods: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go#L73-L77.

This is problematic for jobs, which as a workaround categorizes all deleted pods (with `deletionTimestamp != nil`) as failed,
but it is still problematic:
- the replacement pod is created too early, leaving two running pods (for the same index) at the same time, which is a problem for some job frameworks. See related Issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115844.
- a pod categorized a failed by the job controller (due to the presence of deletionTimestamp) may end up succeeded if the pod's container completes successfully within the graceful termination period. 
- it blocks a related issue in Jobs: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113855.

The solution might be scoped to pods with finalizers to save a PATCH request to make the transitioning. 

Fixing this issue is planned as part of the Jobs KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3329

### What 
ROOT CAUSE: The kubelet did not transition deleted pods that are still in the Running or Pending phase to a terminal phase (Succeeded or Failed) even when their containers had terminated and would not be restarted due to their RestartPolicy. This caused deleted pods to remain stuck in Running or Pending state indefinitely.
FIX: Give terminal phase correctly to all pods that will not be restarted. 

In particular, assign Failed phase to pods which are deleted while pending. Also, assign a terminal 
phase (Succeeded or Failed, depending on the exit statuses of the pod containers) to pods which
are deleted while running.

This fixes the issue for jobs using pod failure policy (with JobPodFailurePolicy and PodDisruptionConditions 
feature gates enabled) that their pods could get stuck in the pending phase when deleted.

ACTION REQUIRED: Users who maintain controllers which relied on the fact that pods with RestartPolicy=Always
never enter the Succeeded phase may need to adapt their controllers. This is because as a consequence of 
the change pods which use RestartPolicy=Always may end up in the Succeeded phase in two scenarios: pod 
deletion and graceful node shutdown.

Deployed a statefulset with `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` and with `minReadySeconds: 15`, have waited for all the pods being ready. Then, issued a rollout restart on the sts.

### What did you expect to happen?

Expected that the rollout update happens the same way as with `podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady`, that is the last pod is terminated, then restarted, waited to be ready, and then waiting for the extra `minReadySeconds` to pass before moving the next pod.     metadata:

    spec:
      containers:
      - image: nginx
        name: web
  updateStrategy:

```

TITLE: StatefulSet with `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` should create pods in parallel
SYMPTOM: ### What would you like to be added?

When `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` is set, StatefulSetController should issue create requests for replicas in batches (similar to how other controllers work, e.g. ReplicaSetController) when creating pods for the first time and scaling up.

### Why is this needed?

Currently even with `Parallel` podManagementPolicy StatefulSet the replicas are still _created_ sequentially, even though they can start to _run_ in any order.

This severely limits pod throughput when working with large StatefulSets (~thousands of replicas). For example, 10 StatefulSets with 5k pods each achieve a total of ~6 pods/s, while 1k StatefulSets with 50 pods each allows for creating ~120 pods/s. 

`Parallel` policy suggests the pods can be created sequentially (https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/stateful-set-v1/#StatefulSetSpec): 

>The alternative policy is Parallel which will create pods in parallel to match the desired scale without waiting, and on scale down will delete all pods at once.

Relevant code (`Parallel` policy controls the value of `monotonic`): https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/s
ROOT CAUSE: The StatefulSet controller's implementation incorrectly creates pods sequentially even when the `podManagementPolicy` is set to `Parallel`. This goes against the policy's intention that pods can be created concurrently, resulting in performance bottlenecks for large StatefulSets due to unnecessary serialization of pod creation requests.
FIX: Faster StatefulSet creation when `Parallel` mode is enabled.

TITLE: Memory leak in kubelet volume_manager populator processedPods
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

If a pod is created and then deleted an entry in processedPods map remains forever (sometimes, it's racy).

The problem comes from the fact that `podWorker` calls volume_manager `WaitForUnmount()` asynchronously. If the last call happens after populator cleaned up resources, an entry is added to processedPods and will never be seen.

### What did you expect to happen?

An entry in processedPods map must be deleted if pod doesn't exist and pod runtime should removed according to `dswp.podStateProvider`.

triage.summary: Garbage collector incorrectly deletes a DaemonSet after its ownerReference is updated to a new owner and the old owner is deleted, indicating a race condition between ownerReference update and GC's existence check of owners.

evidence.text:
Garbage collector deletes DaemonSet after updating ownerReference and deleting previous owner
### What happened?

In rare cases, I'm seeing the GC deleting a DaemonSet with a valid ownerReference. This issue looks like a time-of-check/time-of-use error in the garbage collector, although I'm unsure from the docs what behavior to expect.

I'm using a tool similar to `kubectl apply --prune`, called `synk`, except instead of using a label selector to prune old resources, it uses the Kubernetes garbage collector. However, I've found that some systems (single-node test clusters on VMs) break after a reboot, due to unexpected deletion of a DaemonSet. Strangely, I've not seen any other resources getting deleted (even DaemonSets in other manifests installed the same way), so I'm not sure what's special about this DaemonSet.

The order of events, when using this to install a manifest for kube-proxy, is as follows:

- setup (working as intended)
  - synk creates a new owner custom resource (the `ResourceSet`), kube-proxy.v1
  - synk creates the resources in the manifest, including the `kube-proxy` DaemonSet
- update (not always working)
  - synk creates a new owner custom resource (the `ResourceSet`), kube-proxy.v2
  - synk patches the `kube-proxy` DaemonSet to update its ownerReference to point to kube-proxy.v1
  - synk deletes the old owner, kube-proxy.v1
  - sometimes, the garbage collector deletes the DaemonSet, even though it still has a valid ownerReference

### What did you expect to happen?

The garbage collector should only delete resources with dangling ow

diagnosis.root_cause: The garbage collector fetches the latest ownerReferences of an object and decides deletion based on this state, but between fetching and deletion it does not reverify ownerReferences. This race condition allows deletion of a resource if its ownerReference changes after the fetch but before deletion, since GC only checks the object's UID precondition and not resourceVersion, causing broken consistency and mistaken deletion of objects that now have a valid owner.

claims.text: The GC fetches the latest ownerReferences of the object at line 512, then checks owners at line 544, but deletes the object at line 615 without re-checking if ownerReferences changed, enabling a race between checking and deleting.
The deletion is done with a UID precondition but without resourceVersion precondition, so it cannot prevent lost updates if the ownerReference is changed right after fetching and before deletion.

The user report and audit logs show that the GC deletes a DaemonSet even though it has a valid updated ownerReference, consistent with a TOCTOU race in the GC's deletion logic due to ownerReference update and old owner deletion interleaving.

diagnosis.root_cause: The rollout controller enqueues ReplicaSet availability checks only when a pod transitions from not ready to ready, ignoring pods that are ready but still within the minReadySeconds delay or pods that restart during this delay. This causes the rollout status check to hang or time out when pods restart before minReadySeconds elapse, as the controller never schedules a recheck after the pod's availability actually becomes valid.

claims.text: The code snippet in the ReplicaSet controller re-enqueues the ReplicaSet for an availability check only if a pod goes from not ready to ready and MinReadySeconds is set; it does not handle the case where a pod is already ready but not available due to minReadySeconds or pod restarts within minReadySeconds.

The IsPodAvailable function returns true only if a pod is ready and has been so for at least minReadySeconds, meaning a pod that is ready but still within minReadySeconds is considered unavailable, which the ReplicaSet controller does not re-check properly.

The observed failure mode with Deployment rollout hangs or exceeds progress deadlines when minReadySeconds is set and a pod restarts during rollout is documented in the ticket and reproduced by using kubectl rollout restart; the rollout never succeeds without a deletion of the pod or leader election restart.

TITLE: removeMissingExtendedResources() did not remove unknown extension resources from InitContainer
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The function removeMissingExtendedResources() located at pkg/kubelet/lifecycle/predicate.go:217, is designed to remove any extended resources from a container’s requests that are not found in nodeInfo.Allocatable before the pod is admitted. This is necessary to support cluster-level resources, which are extended resources that are unknown to nodes.
However, this function only removes missingExtendedResources from the container’s requests, and does not process the requests of initContainers. This could lead to issues, as initContainers might request resources that do not exist on the node, which could result in the pod failing to be admitted or other unforeseen issues. As such, it may be necessary to refine the removeMissingExtendedResources() function to also handle initContainer’s requests.

### What did you expect to happen?

Refine the removeMissingExtendedResources() function to also handle initContainer’s requests.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a pod that requests cluster-level extended resources in both the container and InitContainer.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes versi
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug was that the removeMissingExtendedResources() function was incomplete in its processing scope; it only sanitized the extended resource requests of regular containers but neglected to perform the same cleanup for initContainers. Since initContainers can also request extended resources unknown to the node, this omission led to potential resource mismatches and pod admission failures.
FIX: Remove missing extended resources from init containers

TITLE: endpoints not configured with MinimizeIPTablesRestore
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

While the version in 1.26 is still alpha I have not found any significant changes, bug reports or backports in the changelog regarding this.

It seems sometimes kube-proxy does not see that the endpoints of a service need to be updated despite the api endpointslice having changed. This typically is not that visible with externalTrafficPolicy Cluster services as some other endpoint still is configured, but in the case of low replica services or externalTrafficPolicy Local services this can lead to service disruption due to the only endpoint on the local node not getting configured while other components see the update correctly and direct traffic there.

that could result in some updates getting lost (e.g., when a service gets a

TITLE:  kube-proxy: traffic to healthcheck host ports is dropped because of iptables rule order
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We are running self managed Kubernetes clusters on GCP and use Services of `type: LoadBalancer` with both public and private `EXTERNAL-IP`s to create load balancers for our clusters. Since upgrading kube-proxy to 1.26.3 (from 1.25.5) we saw that all healthchecks from GCP started to fail and traffic is now blindly load balanced across all nodes, which broke Services with
`externalTrafficPolicy` set to `Local`.
The issue seems to be introduced with this change: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/108460
Here, `KUBE-IPVS-IPS` ipset is introduced and is used in iptables on chain `KUBE-IPVS-FILTER` as:

A new  kube-proxyvalidation introduced in k8s 1.28 seems to break Azure + ipv6. IPv6 clusters on Azure run on dual-stack hosts. The IPv6 node IP seems like it's only getting assigned to the Node until after kube-proxy starts (someone might need to help me understand what component is responsible). However, kube-proxy now fails to start with:

kube-proxy is in CrashloopBackoff, logs show:

``` 
I0825 16:18:19.872382       1 server_others.go:69] "Using iptables proxy"

TITLE: Document and test minimum privileges needed to run kube-proxy
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Running containers in privileged mode is not recommended as privileged containers run with all [linux capabilities](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/capabilities.7.html) enabled and can access the host's resources. Running containers in privileged mode opens number of security threads such as breakout to underlying host OS.

Currently the kube-proxy DaemonSet runs in privileged mode.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/863a462eeccca4c24bf4c4e9012f5ebccade70a2/cluster/addons/kube-proxy/kube-proxy-ds.yaml#L50-L51

https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/kubelet-in-userns/#configuring-kube-proxy describes how to run kube-proxy in "rootless". To my understanding "rootless" != non-privileged mode but this configuration can be also used for running in non-privileged mode. However I see that following issues with it:
1. In the provided kube-proxy component config in https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/kubelet-in-userns/#configuring-kube-proxy we have to disable certain settins to prevent kube-proxy from ensuring sysctls (which is allowed only in privileged container).

But when I tried to run kube-proxy with the prov
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because kube-proxy requires setting certain sysctls that need privileged container mode, but there was no mechanism to run these privileged operations separately from the main non-privileged kube-proxy process. This forced kube-proxy to run fully privileged or fail when run with lowered privileges, with no way to disable these sysctl settings via configuration.
FIX: Added a new `--init-only` command line flag to `kube-proxy`. Setting the flag makes `kube-proxy` perform its initial configuration that requires privileged mode, and then exit. The `--init-only` mode is intended to be executed in a privileged init container, so that the main container may run with a stricter `securityContext`.
FILES: cmd/kube-proxy/app/server.go, cmd/kube-proxy/app/server_others.go, cmd/kube-proxy/app/server_windows.go, pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go, pkg/proxy/ipvs/proxier.go, pkg/proxy/kubemark/hollow_proxy.go

TITLE: kube-proxy healthcheck all zero listening
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I have deployed a Kubernetes cluster with version 1.28 in a dual-stack environment. The main configuration for kube-proxy is as follows:
```yaml
...
--cluster-cidr=172.22.0.0/16,1111::/48
--nodeport-addresses=192.168.30.0/24
...
```
Then, I deployed a service with healthCheckNodePort: 30955 and other settings as follows:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-deploy-svc
spec:
  healthCheckNodePort: 30955
  ipFamilyPolicy: PreferDualStack
  type: LoadBalancer
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
...
```
However, port 30955 is listening on all zeros, as shown below:
```shell
tcp6       0      0 :::30955                :::*                    LISTEN      110720/kube-proxy
```
When I restarted kube-proxy, the all-zeros listening issue was resolved, and it now looks like this:
```shell
tcp        0      0 192.168.30.89:30955      0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      25411/kube-proxy
```
I would like to know whether, in a dual-stack environment, to achieve non-all-zeros listening, both IPv4 and IPv6 address ranges must be configured for the `--nodeport-addresses` parameter. Otherwise, it may lead to the all-zeros listening issue
ROOT CAUSE: The kube-proxy component lacked a properly configured --nodeport-addresses setting in a dual-stack environment, causing it to listen on all IP interfaces (0.0.0.0 and ::) by default. This results in healthCheckNodePort binding to all zeros (wildcard address) instead of a node's specific IP, because the code defaults to listening on all addresses if no specific nodeport address ranges are configured.
FIX: The kube-proxy nodeportAddresses / --nodeport-addresses option now
accepts the value "primary", meaning to only listen for NodePort connections
on the node's primary IPv4 and/or IPv6 address (according to the Node object).
This is strongly recommended, if you were not previously using
--nodeport-addresses, to avoid surprising behavior.

(This behavior is enabled by default with the nftables backend; you would
need to explicitly request `--nodeport-addresses 0.0.0.0/0,::/0` there to get
the traditional "listen on all interfaces" behavior.)
FILES: cmd/kube-proxy/app/server.go, cmd/kube-proxy/app/server_linux.go, cmd/kube-proxy/app/server_test.go, pkg/generated/openapi/zz_generated.openapi.go, pkg/proxy/apis/config/types.go, pkg/proxy/apis/config/validation/validation.go, pkg/proxy/apis/config/validation/validation_test.go, pkg/proxy/apis/config/zz_generated.deepcopy.go, pkg/proxy/healthcheck/healthcheck_test.go, pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go

diagnosis.root_cause: kube-proxy calls utiliptables.NewDualStack() which returns an error when only one IP family (IPv4 or IPv6) is supported; this causes platformCheckSupported to return an error and kube-proxy fails to start on single-stack hosts instead of tolerating single-stack operation.

claims.text: The function platformCheckSupported in cmd/kube-proxy/app/server_linux.go calls utiliptables.NewDualStack(), which returns an error if only one IP family is supported, causing kube-proxy to fail start on single-stack hosts.

The regression was introduced in PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131534 that returns error if not both IPv4 and IPv6 work and was explained in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132170, confirmed by ticket report.
The user environment described in the ticket runs single-stack IPv4 only VM, so the call to NewDualStack fails and prevents kube-proxy from starting.

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug is caused by the Allocator struct's field claimsToAllocate being shared and written concurrently by multiple goroutines during calls to the Allocate method without synchronization. TITLE: [Bug] Missing constraint and validation for label selector's values
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Hello,
There are some [constraints](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/#syntax-and-character-set) that label selector's `values` need to conform:
>* must be 63 characters or less (can be empty),
>* unless empty, must begin and end with an alphanumeric character ([a-z0-9A-Z]),
>* could contain dashes (-), underscores (_), dots (.), and alphanumerics between.

Every label selctor's `values` will be checked [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e5ba5cd2b0d3bddd4a0393b98fde14960f31a33c/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/validation/validation.go#L166C1-L175C2), and when values is not conforming these constraints, an error will be returned.

`nodeAfffinty.requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution.nodeSelectorTerms.matchExpressions.values` also needs to conform these constraints (because `matchExpressions` will be parsed as a label selector), but cccording to the [concept documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#operators) and the [API documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/v1.31/#nodeselectorrequirement-v1-core), 
ROOT CAUSE: The underlying cause is that the system did not validate the values in NodeSelectorRequirement against label value constraints during pod creation. This lack of validation allowed invalid strings to be accepted, leading to parse errors during scheduling and causing the scheduler to reject the node selector terms silently without warning the user.
FIX: kubenetes starts validating NodeSelectorRequirement's values when creating pods.
FILES: pkg/api/node/util.go, pkg/api/persistentvolume/util.go, pkg/api/pod/util.go, pkg/api/pod/util_test.go, pkg/api/pod/warnings.go, pkg/api/pod/warnings_test.go, pkg/apis/core/helper/helpers.go, pkg/apis/core/helper/helpers_test.go, pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go, pkg/apis/core/validation/validation_test.go

TITLE: Memory leak in kubelet volume_manager populator processedPods
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

If a pod is created and then deleted an entry in processedPods map remains forever (sometimes, it's racy).

The problem comes from the fact that `podWorker` calls volume_manager `WaitForUnmount()` asynchronously. If the last call happens after populator cleaned up resources, an entry is added to processedPods and will never be seen.

### What did you expect to happen?

An entry in processedPods map must be deleted if pod doesn't exist and pod runtime should removed according to `dswp.podStateProvider`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To verify that the issue really exists I applaied a simple [patch](https://github.com/jsafrane/kubernetes/commit/40ffc8e62836244ea6cffde8b9dff2c402d058c5) printing resources in `processedPods` map. Here is a reproducer:

2. Check entries in `processedPods`:
```
I0321 15:03:42.131049    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:264] JSAF: processed pod ac109c78-ce77-4426-9421-53fbcfe2175b: true
I0321 15:03:43.131815    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:262] JSAF: processed pods size: 1
```
3. Create a pod, chec
ROOT CAUSE: The volume_manager's podWorker calls WaitForUnmount asynchronously. If the final asynchronous call happens after the populator has cleaned up its resources, a pod UID is added to the processedPods map but the populator no longer tracks that pod. This pod entry then remains in processedPods indefinitely because the cleanup code only processes pods currently tracked by the volume_manager's internal cache.
FIX: Fix memory leak in kubelet volume_manager populator processedPods

diagnosis.root_cause: The SELinux warning controller uses a SELinuxTranslator that incorrectly treats empty SELinux label components as non-conflicting, resulting in missed conflict detection when comparing a pod's SELinux label with defaulted (empty) components against another pod's label with explicit components, such as the SELinux level. This defect arises because the controller runs in kube-controller-manager which lacks knowledge of OS defaults and thus skips meaningful comparison of empty label parts, unlike kubelet which defaults these components and detects conflict correctly.

claims.text: The SELinuxTranslator Conflicts method treats empty SELinux label components as incomparable and does not report conflicts if either label part is empty, ignoring differences in parts such as the SELinux level.

The volume cache AddVolume method uses the SELinuxTranslator to detect conflicts between pod volumes, but because of the translator's logic, it misses conflicts when one label is empty in some components and the other is not, causing missing conflict reports in the SELinux warning controller.

The SELinux warning controller runs in kube-controller-manager which does not know OS default SELinux label components and skips comparison of empty components, unlike kubelet which defaults empty components and reports conflicts correctly.

TITLE: DaemonSet fails to scale down during the rolling update when `maxUnavailable=0`
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I have a daemonset with the rolling update strategy. I have `maxSurge` parameter set to a non zero value [which means](https://github.com/openshift/kubernetes/blob/cb4b47e5ddfbaf7844237b2e2eb2b0acfed5f1b5/pkg/apis/apps/validation/validation.go#L394-L402) that the `maxUnavailable` parameter is set to `0`. When I replace the toleration in the daemonset's template spec from the one which helped me to be scheduled on the master node into any other toleration, I see the new pods still trying to be scheduled on the master nodes. The old pods from the tolerated nodes can be lucky enough to be recreated but only if they go before any pod from the intolerable node.

```
$ kubectl -n openshift-dns get ds dns-default -o yaml | yq .spec.updateStrategy
rollingUpdate:
  maxSurge: 10%
  maxUnavailable: 0
type: RollingUpdate

$ kubectl -n openshift-dns get ds dns-default -o yaml | yq .spec.template.spec.tolerations
- key: node-role.kubernetes.io/master
  operator: Exists
  
$ kubectl -n openshift-dns get pods  -o wide | grep dns-default
dns-default-6bfmf     2/2     Running   0          119m    10.129.0.40   ci-ln-sb5ply2-72292-qlhc8-master-2         <none>     
ROOT CAUSE: The daemonset rolling update logic included all nodes with existing pods for updating regardless of whether the new daemonset's tolerations matched the nodes' taints. This caused new pods to be scheduled on intolerable nodes and the old pods on tolerable nodes not to be deleted, leading to the update being stuck when maxUnavailable was 0.
FIX: Revised the logic for DaemonSet rolling update to exclude nodes if scheduling constraints are not met.
This eliminates the problem of rolling updates to a DaemonSet getting stuck around tolerations.
FILES: pkg/controller/daemon/update.go, pkg/controller/daemon/update_test.go, test/integration/daemonset/daemonset_test.go

TITLE: Pod Garbage collector fails to clean up  PODs from nodes that are not running anymore
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

This happened after upgrading to Kubernetes 1.26 from 1.24

The succession of events we have observed:
- Our workloads use HorizontalPodAutoscaler to scale up due to traffic increase
- Cluster Autoscaler provisions new nodes to accommodate the new replicas
- Traffic goes down
- HPA downsize replicas
- Cluster Autoscaler notices nodes under the threshold of usage and PODs can be accommodated into other nodes
- Nodes are drained and downscaled
- Kubernetes still reports PODs in a "Running" or "Terminating" state in the node that no longer exists
- Kubernetes control plane reports "Orphan pods" on its audit logs

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubernetes Garbage collector to clean up these PODs after the node is gone

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Deploy the following yaml deployments into a K8s cluster 1.26 and terminate one of the nodes

(duplicated port key "containerPort + protocol")
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: nginx
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: nginx
    app.kubernetes.io/component: deployment
spec:
  
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug is a regression introduced by enabling PodDisruptionConditions by default. This caused the pod garbage collector to fail deleting pods that had duplicated fields such as repeated environment variable keys or container ports, resulting in orphan pods left on non-existent nodes. The garbage collector used Server-Side Apply (SSA) for patching Pod Disruption Conditions, which failed on pods with duplicated fields, blocking cleanup.
FIX: Fixed a regression in default configurations, which enabled PodDisruptionConditions by default, 
that prevented the control plane's pod garbage collector from deleting pods that contained duplicated field keys (env. variables with repeated keys or container ports).

SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs due to inadequate error handling in the delete request decoding process: when the DeleteOptions decoding fails due to type mismatches or incorrect values in request parameters, the API server returns a 500 Internal Server Error instead of a 400 Bad Request. This happens because the decoding from the request body uses a decoder that returns decoding errors directly (resulting in 5xx errors), instead of treating them as client errors, unlike parameter decoding which returns 400 for bad requests.

claims.text: The ticket shows that passing incorrectly typed parameters in a DELETE request results in 500 errors, including type mismatch errors and conversion errors for DeleteOptions.

The code in staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/handlers/delete.go decodes DeleteOptions from the request body and if a decoding error occurs there, it returns the error directly, which causes 5xx responses instead of returning a 400 Bad Request error as is done for query parameter decoding errors.

TITLE: HPA metric got stuck at a random value and not scaling down after reaching max replica count
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I utilize two customized metrics, A and B, in my HPA system. A is a gauge-based metric called SLA Metric, while B is a count-based metric that tracks failed requests with HTTP status code 502 or 503 from Istio. These metrics are scraped by Prometheus.

To use custom metrics in HPA, we're employing Kube Metrics Adapter [link](https://github.com/zalando-incubator/kube-metrics-adapter). When the application load increases, the value of the SLA Metric also increases, and then the pods scale up until they reach the maximum replica count as expected.
However, the problem arises when the load dissipates, and the pods never scale down. Despite the SLA Metric's value being below the target in Prometheus, the HPA description still displays the metric value with a stale value that can be above or below the target.

One possible reason for this is that Metric B, which relies on Istio requests, shows up as unknown since there have been no failed requests with the 502 or 503 status codes. Thus, the Prometheus query fails.
We have noticed this behavior after upgrading Kube from version 1.21 to 1.24 and changing the HPA version from autoscaling/v2beta2 to autoscaling/v2
ROOT CAUSE: The HPA controller had an edge case where if a custom metric became unavailable (returned as unknown), the controller would not update the status metrics while updating the replica count. diagnosis.root_cause: The HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) replica count calculation converts a floating-point usage ratio, which can be arbitrarily large due to external metric values divided by small thresholds, directly into a 32-bit integer. This cast can overflow the maximum int32 limit (2147483647), causing wraparound to negative values and resulting in the HPA scaling down to the minimum replica count inaccurately. This overflow defect is due to unsafe casting from float64 to int32 in the replica calculation logic without adequate bounds checking or saturation.

claims.text: The root cause is an integer overflow when converting a large floating-point replica count to int32 in the replica_calculator.go file, causing negative values and erroneous scaling.

An external metric exceeding 214,748,364 combined with a threshold of 0.1 results in a usage ratio large enough that when multiplied by the number of ready pods and cast to int32, it overflows, triggering the bug.
The specific calculation involved is in getUsageRatioReplicaCount where usageRatio * readyPodCount (both float64) is cast to int32 without checks, permitting overflow.

TITLE: Mismatched URLs for service-account-issuer-discovery and Open API Spec's swagger.json
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When I use the official Kubernetes Java Client (version 18.0.0) from within a pod using `Config.defaultClient()` to build an `ApiClient` and then access `getServiceAccountIssuerOpenIDConfiguration` in the `WellKnownApi` I get the following error:

```json
{
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "forbidden: User \"system:serviceaccount:test:user\" cannot get path \"/.well-known/openid-configuration/\"",
  "reason": "Forbidden",
  "details": {},
  "code": 403
}
```

The same happens with the `OpenidApi#getServiceAccountIssuerOpenIDKeyset`.

However, the problem does not happen when I call the `/.well-known/openid-configuration` endpoint using the pod's service account and curl.

The problem is that the generated Open API spec indicates that the client should call `/.well-known/openid-configuration/` instead of `/.well-known/openid-configuration` (and similarly `/openid/v1/jwks/` instead of `/openid/v1/jwks`). While the API Server seems to resolve these endpoints just fine, the `ClusterRole` defined in the code does not have the trailing slashes and therefore rejects the requests with a 
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the ClusterRole for service-account-issuer-discovery defines permissions for nonResourceURLs without trailing slashes, but the OpenAPI spec (swagger.json) documents these URLs with trailing slashes. This mismatch causes RBAC authorization to fail for legally formed requests that append a trailing slash, since the policy does not allow those exact paths.
FIX: Add slash ended urls for service-account-issuer-discovery to match API in swagger
FILES: plugin/pkg/auth/authorizer/rbac/bootstrappolicy/policy.go, plugin/pkg/auth/authorizer/rbac/bootstrappolicy/testdata/cluster-roles.yaml

diagnosis.root_cause: The warning about spec.SessionAffinity being ignored for headless services is printed whenever SessionAffinity is not an empty string. claims.text: The warning is printed whenever SessionAffinity is not an empty string for headless services, as seen in the conditional in pkg/api/service/warnings.go that triggers the warning when service.Spec.SessionAffinity != "".

The ticket explains that the warning gets printed for headless services without a user-defined SessionAffinity value because the default value is "None", which cannot be distinguished from an explicitly set value, causing erroneous warnings.

triage.summary: In Kubernetes 1.34, kubelet's gRPC connections to the NVIDIA DRA plugin hang after going idle, causing pods with DRA resources to remain stuck in Terminating state; the expected behavior is for connections to handle idle timeouts gracefully without blocking pod termination.

evidence.text:
Regression 1.34 -- Kubelet requires restart after gRPC connection to DRA driver goes idle
This issue describes a bug in DRA's plugin communication with the kubelet that causes pods to get stuck in the Terminating state. This only occurs after waiting a *long* time (in my original test case 75 minutes).

After some testing, I've concluded that this occurs when gRPC connections to DRA plugins go idle after their configured timeout period. The issue becomes reproducible after 1 minute by shortening the idle timeout to 1 minute using `grpc.WithIdleTimeout(time.Minute)`, showing that the problem is related to gRPC's idle connection handling.

Once we reach this point where the gRPC connection has gone idle, attempting to terminate a pod with DRA allocated resourcces hang during cleanup, with the kubelet logging `Calling NodeUnprepareResource rpc` but never logging the corresponding `Done calling` message. The gRPC calls to the DRA plugin never complete despite having a 45-second context timeout.

Note, that The DRA plugin never receives the `NodeUnprepareResources` requests that kubelet claims to be sending. This indicates that the hang occurs after the kubelet sends the request but before it reaches the plugin, pointing to an issue in gRPC's internal connection management.

The only current workaround for users is to restart kubelet, which forces fresh connection establishment and resolves the stuck pods until the next idle timeout period expires.

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug happens because the kubelet's DRA plugin gRPC client connection goes idle after a configured timeout and gRPC internal connection management fails to correctly handle these idle connections, causing them to hang indefinitely for subsequent RPC calls like NodeUnprepareResources. In particular, after the idle timeout, RPC calls made by kubelet never complete and do not reach the plugin, resulting in stuck pod termination and no retry or reconnection occurs automatically before the RPC call. This leads to the kubelet needing a restart to refresh connections and resolve the hang.

claims.text: The kubelet calls NodeUnprepareResources RPC on DRA plugins via gRPC, expecting calls to complete or error. When gRPC connection has gone idle after the timeout, calls hang and never complete, causing pods to get stuck terminating.

The gRPC client connection to the DRA plugin is created without explicit idle timeout configuration in the original code, matching the scenario where idle connections cause hangs; enabling the ResourceHealthStatus feature gate avoids the hang by maintaining persistent streams that keep connections active.

The DRA plugin manager uses a grpcstats handler to detect connection begin and end events and attempts to reconnect on connection end, but there is no explicit recreation or validation of connection state before each RPC call, leaving a window where idle connections are not recovered.

TITLE: KeyEncipherment usage should not be required for non-RSA kubelet client/serving CSRs
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

https://github.com/golang/go/issues/36499 describes why the KeyEncipherment extended key usage does not make sense (and in some cases, is not allowed) for ECDSA keys.

The Kubernetes `kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving` and `kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client-kubelet` signer names require a `key encipherment` usage.

If the kubelet is not using an RSA key (which it does not [by default](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.23.0/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/certificate/certificate_manager.go#L640-L642)), it should not need to specify this key usage.

Since relaxing this to make the `key encipherment` usage optional for those two signerNames may involve an API validation change, this may need rollout over 2 releases. The places we'll need to make sure work properly are:

1. API validation of CSR create and update requests
2. Controller tolerating CSR objects with/without that usage
3. Kubelets requesting CSRs properly without that usage if given a non-RSA key

### What did you expect to happen?

n/a

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

n/a

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes v
ROOT CAUSE: The Kubernetes CSR API required the KeyEncipherment usage for kubelet client and serving certificates regardless of the key type. However, this key usage does not apply to ECDSA keys (which are the default for kubelet), making the requirement incorrect and causing validation failures or unnecessary constraints when non-RSA keys are used.
FIX: Relax API validation for usage key encipherment and kubelet uses requested usages accordingly

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the statsCache's prefix is empty for certain storage keys such as "/masterleases/192.168.0.1", leading to malformed or empty keys after the cleanKeys function attempts to ensure keys have the prefix. claims.text: The error message 'Error getting keys' with err='empty key: ""' is logged from cleanKeysIfNeeded where the GetKeys method is called for a keys list, and the error originates there.

The cleanKeys method modifies keys by adding a prefix if missing; if the prefix is empty (sc.prefix == ""), keys like '/masterleases/192.168.0.1' will have this prefix insertion logic create empty or malformed keys, leading to subsequent errors.

The ticket states that some resources such as 'masterleases' use keys with full paths but no prefix, which means statsCache is constructed with an empty prefix, which triggers the problem in cleanKeys when it tries to prepend an empty prefix to keys lacking it.

TITLE: CRD validation allows invalid CABundles that will fail setting up handlers
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

A CRDs with an invalid conversion webhook CABundle failed to serve requests not requiring conversion.

### What did you expect to happen?

Since creating cr-1.yaml doesn't require conversion, I would have expected either:

1. An error response when attempting to create/update the CRD with an invalid CABundle
2. Only an error when conversion is required to server a request

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?


Create a mult-version CRD with a conversion webhook configured with an invalid CABundle:

```yaml
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: replicant.stable.example.com
spec:
  group: stable.example.com
  versions:
    - name: v1
      served: true
      storage: true
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              properties:
                myfield:
                  type: integer
    - name: v2
      served: true
      storage: false
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              ty
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the CRD validation logic allowed invalid or non-PEM-encoded CABundles to be accepted when creating or updating CustomResourceDefinitions. This caused failures later when setting up conversion webhook handlers, which expect a valid CA certificate bundle for secure communication. Without proper validation at CRD creation time, invalid CABundles lead to internal errors and prevented serving requests properly.
FIX: CustomResourceDefinition objects created with non-empty `caBundle` fields which are invalid or do not contain any certificates will not appear in discovery or serve endpoints until a valid `caBundle` is provided. Updates to CustomResourceDefinition are no longer allowed to transition a valid `caBundle` field to an invalid `caBundle` field, because this breaks serving of the existing CustomResourceDefinition.

ROOT CAUSE: The validation logic for finalizer names was applied differently between Custom Resources and builtin resource types. TITLE: Kubectl restmapping cache causes inconsistent behaviour in case of resource name conflict
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I deployed a CRD (`teleportroles`) with the shortnames `role` and `roles`, conflicting with `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1`.

Initially `kubectl get role` and `kubectl get roles` were both returnning `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1` resources.

I ran `kubectl get teleportrole`.

Now, `kubectl get role` return my CRs instead of `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1` resources.

However `kubectl get roles` continues to return `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1` resources.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect kubectl's behaviour to be consistent. The outcome of `kubectl get X` should not depend on the order the APIs were discovered and cached. I also expect exact names to be preferred over shortnames.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On a freshly kubectl context (not one you already used and might have cached RESTMappings):
- create a CRD with a shortname conflicting with another resource, `role` for example
- run `kubectl get role -n kube-sytem` (because there are roles by default there) and `kubectl get roles -n kube-system`
- observe the kube rbac resources are properly returned
- run `kubectl g
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that core Kubernetes resource types lacked singular names in their API discovery metadata, unlike CRDs. This omission caused the discovery client cache to prefer a CRD's shortname over the equivalent core resource singular name, leading to inconsistent RESTMapping resolution depending on the order resources were cached and fetched. Without singular names set for core types, the cache could be overwritten unpredictably when a CRD sharing a shortname was queried first.
FIX: Set singular names for core types to pass to discovery

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the CRD validation warning logic only recognizes string-type format values and does not account for valid numeric formats such as "int32", "int64", "float", and "double". This is due to the validated formats list being limited to string formats, causing numeric formats to be incorrectly flagged as unrecognized during validation of CRD schemas.

claims.text: The recognized formats for CRD validation are declared only for string types and include formats like "email", "hostname", "ipv4", etc., but do not include numeric formats such as "int32", "int64", "float", or "double".

The function that collects unrecognized formats traverses CRD schema properties and matches their formats against the recognized formats list from the validation package, so formats absent from that list such as numeric ones are treated as unrecognized.

The ticket identifies the problem as valid numeric formats "int32", "int64", "float", and "double" being flagged as unrecognized warnings due to the validation logic's limited formats list, confirming that the issue is a defect in the allowed formats recognition mechanism.

TITLE: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Backoff problem when quickly reverting resize patch
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

While working on #125202 , issue with backoff was discovered resulting to slow reconcile when quickly reverting resize patch. This can be reproduced please check https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/125205#issuecomment-2203184854 ,  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/125205#issuecomment-2143527472.

Backoff issue does not happen on v1.30 or older please check https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/125205#issuecomment-2203224319

### What did you expect to happen?

After patching forwards and patching backwards a pod which has a container whose `resizePolicy` is `RestartContainer`and a container whose `restartPolicy`is `RestartContainer` , pod should reach its initial state without any backoff delay introduced.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

<details>

```console
for l in `seq 301 310`; do kubectl patch pod resize-pod --patch "{\"spec\":{\"containers\":[{\"name\":\"c2\", \"resources\":{\"limits\":{\"memory\":\"${l}Mi\"}}}]}}"; sleep 3; done

NAME         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
resize-pod   3/3     Running   0          14s
resize-pod   3/3 
ROOT CAUSE: The bug was caused because the backoff delay for container restarts was not reset when the pod's resource resize patch was quickly reverted. This led to a slow reconcile process due to the backoff mechanism still being in effect, even though the container state returned to the initial state.
FIX: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Fix backoff problem when quickly reverting resize patch

diagnosis.root_cause: The increased POST latency for events at scale is due to the retry mechanism in the generic Store.Create function when generating names for new objects with GenerateName specified. This retry loop can cause multiple additional attempts and retries on name conflicts, increasing create latency significantly at large scale when many events are being created concurrently with generated names.

claims.text: The regression in POST latency for events creation coincides with changes in the generic registry store's Create method to handle retries when GenerateName is specified, shown by the retry loop up to 8 attempts on AlreadyExists errors.

The affected code includes createWithGenerateNameRetry in store.go which performs retries to generate unique names, which can become expensive at large scale creating many events with generated names.

No other code changes in the commit range relate to event creation or API server registry layers, indicating root cause is likely in this retry logic, causing increased latency for event POST requests at scale.

This can lead to a nil pointer in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/124042 (although that's probably an error because some information is needed) and in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/20d0ab7ae808aaddb1556c3c38ca0607663c50ac/staging/src/k8s.io/kubelet/pkg/apis/dra/v1alpha3/api.pb.go#L255 (happened in practice).

Before the update to 1.29.* the control planes were running with 4GB of memory with the same worklow in the cluster without issues. After the workarround using the feature gate the memory consumption of the whole control plane is not at ~2GB.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Client Version: v1.29
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the memory leak was OpenTelemetry's delegating MeterProvider which, before a real implementation is set, tracks every instrument created without deduplicating repeated creations. TITLE: Discovery memCacheClient has inconsistent error behavior with other DiscoveryInterfaces
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I think this got stale and closed because it was posted on `kubernetes/client-go` but is still very relevant:
https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/issues/745

The [memCacheClient](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/f81a9405fae9d2a97f479bab1ab540fad1d2f178/discovery/cached/memory/memcache.go#L47) created by memory.NewMemCacheClient(...) returns an error when calling ServerResourcesForGroupVersion if the APIResources list returned is empty, as seen here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/6d14209323d355841b67c4d9ca8c22fb1ca930a6/discovery/cached/memory/memcache.go#L214-L216

Our particular case came up due to the `external.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1` API group being registered with the API server, but having no resources.

### What did you expect to happen?

If using [NewMemcachedDiscoveryClient](https://github.com/kubecfg/kubecfg/blob/4b23b794b8281c7886b5fd0bd03d7a38db876c10/cmd/root.go#L425) like [here](https://github.com/kubecfg/kubecfg/blob/4b23b794b8281c7886b5fd0bd03d7a38db876c10/pkg/kubecfg/validate.go#L48) to discover `apiservices` with zero current resources there should not be an error returned.

### How can we reproduce i
ROOT CAUSE: The memCacheClient incorrectly treats an empty resource list in an API group version discovery response as an error, whereas other discovery clients do not. This causes spurious error logging when API groups exist but have no resources, such as aggregated metrics APIs. The root cause is that the memCacheClient implementation does not consistently handle empty resource lists as normal (non-error) responses.
FIX: Fixes a 1.26 regression in client-go discovery handling of empty responses

TITLE: kubelet GetBootTime() could drift backward for 1s
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

There are a few places in kubelet that calls `pkg/kubelet/util`.`GetBootTime()`. One such place is the kubelet `/stats/summary` endpoint where it's getting the node startTime: [ref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.30.0/pkg/kubelet/server/stats/summary.go#L56)

And there's an issue in the [Linux implementation of `GetBootTime`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.31.0/pkg/kubelet/util/boottime_util_linux.go#L30) that the result is not consistent: sometimes it could drift backwards for 1s. This caused problem in certain monitoring systems where the time series database expect timestamps to be monotonically increasing.****

### What did you expect to happen?

`GetBootTime()` to return consistent result everytime it runs, more specifically the kubelet `/stats/summary` endpoint returns a consistent node startTime when kubelet restarts.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

do the following steps multiple times:

- restart kubelet
- do a http get on kubelet /stats/summary endpoint
- observe the `node`.`startTime` field in the response

you will see the node startTime could shift backwards for 1s i
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because GetBootTime() uses the current time with sub-second precision and subtracts the system uptime (which is an integer in seconds), and then truncates the result to the earlier second. When the uptime increments between calling time.Now() and unix.Sysinfo(), this subtraction can produce a result that appears to drift backward by one second.
FIX: fix node start time inconsistency in kubelet
FILES: pkg/kubelet/util/boottime_util_linux.go, pkg/kubelet/util/boottime_util_linux_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug happens because the kubelet shutdown manager invokes systemd-logind configuration reload and immediately queries the updated InhibitDelayMaxSec value without waiting for the reload completion. This leads to a race condition where the property read may still reflect the old value as systemd-logind has not finished reloading, causing kubelet to misinterpret the delay value as insufficient and fail to register the shutdown inhibitor.

claims.text: The kubelet nodeshutdown manager starts by overriding InhibitDelayMaxSec and immediately calls ReloadLogindConf() but does not wait for systemd-logind to finish reloading before re-reading the property value.

Because the reload is asynchronous and the code does not wait, reading the updated inhibit delay can return stale values, causing the manager to fail to update and register the shutdown inhibitor properly.

The ticket reproduces the bug with a program that changes systemd-logind configuration and reloads it, then checks the updated property, observing a low frequency race condition that matches the timing of the kubelet's failure.

<details>
no

ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the Kubelet prematurely marked pods as terminated (Succeeded or Failed) in the API before all containers were fully stopped and prevented from restarting. When serializeImagePulls is set to false and multiple pods start concurrently, the pod startup latency tracker records firstStartedPulling but may never record lastFinishedPulling, leaving it unset (zero time). The calculation subtracts firstStartedPulling from lastFinishedPulling without checking if lastFinishedPulling is zero, resulting in a negative duration.

claims.text: The pod startup latency tracker computes podStartSLOduration by subtracting the image pulling duration (lastFinishedPulling - firstStartedPulling) from the pod start duration without checking if lastFinishedPulling is zero, leading to negative values.
If the RecordImageFinishedPulling is not called, lastFinishedPulling remains zero, which is not validated before the subtraction, causing the negative podStartSLOduration.
Logs show negative podStartSLOduration values when serializeImagePulls is false and many pods start simultaneously, consistent with lastFinishedPulling being zero and unvalidated during subtraction.

triage.summary: Pod status incorrectly shows as 'Completed' when one container (main) exits with error and sidecar container exits successfully; pod status should be 'Error' if any container fails.

evidence.text:
Inconsistent POD status reporting
### What happened?

I run service mesh sidecar (in my case Istio) in PODs that are created/controlled by `Jobs`. "Main" container shuts down the istio sidecar via API call to 127.0.0.1 and exits with an actual application code. The issue is when "main" container finishes with error, POD status often displays `Completed` when called via `kubectl get pod`.
```console
NAME                            READY   STATUS      RESTARTS   AGE
job-istio-proxy-test--1-zdlc6   0/2     Completed   0          47s
```
<details>

```yaml

  conditions:
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2022-01-24T10:04:11Z"
    status: "True"
    type: Initialized
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2022-01-24T10:04:26Z"
    message: 'containers with unready status: [somejob istio-proxy]'
    reason: ContainersNotReady
    status: "False"
    type: Ready
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2022-01-24T10:04:26Z"
    message: 'containers with unready status: [somejob istio-proxy]'
    reason: ContainersNotReady
    status: "False"
    type: ContainersReady
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2022-01-24T10:04:10Z"
    status: "True"

  containerStatuses:
  - containerID: containerd://ccf54140202e07f2bd37151dee171fc744158ff81c4a58426bad0518f8dd6c6d

As a result, pods with at least one container failure but with a last container that completed successfully are erroneously marked as Completed instead of Error.

claims.text: The pod status reason reflects only the last container analyzed in ContainerStatuses and does not consider if any previous container failed, leading to incorrect pod status reporting.

The issue manifests as a pod with one failing container reported as Completed, because the status is derived from the last container's reason, which can be Completed even if an earlier container errored.

TITLE: CRD validation allows invalid CABundles that will fail setting up handlers
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

A CRDs with an invalid conversion webhook CABundle failed to serve requests not requiring conversion.

### What did you expect to happen?

Since creating cr-1.yaml doesn't require conversion, I would have expected either:

1. An error response when attempting to create/update the CRD with an invalid CABundle
2. Only an error when conversion is required to server a request

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?


Create a mult-version CRD with a conversion webhook configured with an invalid CABundle:

```yaml

spec:
  group: stable.example.com

      storage: true
